1.q: An insurer wants a model that estimates the repair cost of each new claim, in pounds. Which type of machine learning task is this?
o: Classification, which assigns each input to a category
Regression, which predicts a continuous numeric value for each input
Clustering, which groups similar inputs together without any labels
Generation, which produces new content resembling its training data
1.why: Predicting a continuous quantity, such as a cost, is regression. Classification predicts categories, and clustering finds groups without labels.

1.q: A security analyst wants to find unusual login patterns but has no labelled examples of attacks. Which approach is MOST suitable?
o: Supervised classification, which first needs examples labelled as attacks
Unsupervised anomaly detection, which finds activity that differs from the norm
A language model fine-tuned only on the company’s public product documentation
Reinforcement learning that rewards the model for blocking every single login
1.why: Without labels, unsupervised methods find patterns and outliers. Supervised learning needs labelled attacks, and the other options don’t address the problem.

1.q: Cloud spending on a company’s GPU training account triples overnight, although no new training jobs were approved. What is the MOST likely explanation to investigate?
o: A scheduled model evaluation that ran for longer than usual overnight
Stolen credentials used to run unauthorised workloads, such as mining
A GPU driver update that now reports usage in a different unit
Routine price rises by the provider during a period of high demand
1.why: GPU capacity is expensive and easy to monetise, so stolen cloud credentials are often used to run cryptomining or other unauthorised jobs. A sudden, unexplained spike in spend is a classic sign and should be investigated as a possible compromise.

1.q: A team adapts a large pre-trained model to classify its own support tickets, using only a few thousand labelled examples. Which idea makes this possible?
o: Reinforcement learning, which rewards the model for each correct action
Transfer learning, which reuses what the model learned earlier
Unsupervised clustering, which groups the tickets without labels
Symbolic rules, which hard-code every ticket category by hand
1.why: Transfer learning reuses general knowledge learned during pre-training, so adapting to a new task needs far less data and compute than training from scratch.

1.q: A fraud model performs poorly on its own training data and on new transactions alike. What is the MOST likely explanation?
o: Overfitting, because it has memorised its training data too closely
Underfitting, because it is too simple to capture the patterns
Data poisoning, because an attacker has corrupted every record
Model collapse, because it trained on its own earlier outputs
1.why: Poor performance on both training and new data points to underfitting. Overfitting shows low training error but much higher error on new data.

1.q: An organisation describes its AI as a supply chain of data, models, tools and services from many parties. Why does this view matter for security?
o: It means the organisation is no longer responsible for any of its AI risks
Each hand-off between parties is a trust boundary that needs its own controls
It shows that only the final model provider ever needs a security review
It removes the need to keep an inventory of the AI systems in use
1.why: Every hand-off, from data sources to model providers to tools, is a point where trust must be verified. Accountability stays with the organisation.

1.q: Staff ask a general-purpose LLM about a company policy introduced last month. It answers confidently, but wrongly. What is the MOST likely cause?
o: The temperature is set much too low for questions about recent events
The policy is newer than its training cut-off and isn’t retrieved
A competitor poisoned the model during its pre-training phase
The request exceeded the context window, so the policy was cut
1.why: A model’s knowledge stops at its training cut-off and excludes internal documents. Without retrieval, it may fill the gap with plausible but wrong answers.

1.q: A RAG assistant finds a passage about “annual leave” when a user asks about “holiday entitlement”. What makes this possible?
o: Keyword matching, which looks for the exact words in the question
Embeddings, which place texts with similar meanings close together
Fine-tuning, which taught the model every policy by heart
Named entity recognition, which labels the people in each passage
1.why: Embeddings map text to vectors so that similar meanings sit close together, enabling semantic search beyond exact keyword matches.

1.q: An assistant answers questions about internal policies by looking up the relevant policy text when each question arrives, and giving it to the model with the question. Which architecture is this?
o: Fine-tuning, which retrains the model on every policy document each night
Retrieval-augmented generation, which adds retrieved passages to the prompt
Reinforcement learning from human feedback, which ranks answers by preference
Transfer learning, which copies a model trained by another organisation
1.why: RAG retrieves relevant content at question time and places it in the model’s context, so answers can draw on current documents without retraining.

1.q: A team is upgrading a customer service chatbot into an agent that can issue refunds and update orders through tools. Which change to the risk assessment is MOST important?
o: Re-rating the chatbot’s hallucination risk on the same basis as before
Treating manipulated outputs as able to trigger actions with real effects
Lowering the risk rating, since tools make the assistant more accurate
Focusing on response time, since each tool call slows down the answers
1.why: Once an assistant can act through tools, a manipulated or mistaken output no longer just produces bad text: it can move money or change records. The assessment must cover tool permissions, approvals and injection paths.

1.q: A vendor markets its open-weight model as “70B”. When planning to self-host it, what does this figure MOST likely describe?
o: It was trained on about 70 billion documents from across the public web
It has about 70 billion parameters, the weights learned in training
It can accept about 70 billion tokens in one request at a time
It needs about 70 billion bytes of memory for every user request
1.why: The figure refers to parameters, the learned weights. Parameter count drives memory and compute needs: at 16-bit precision, each weight takes two bytes.

1.q: A team wants an assistant to analyse a 600-page manual in a single request. Which model property limits this MOST directly?
o: Its temperature, which controls how random the sampling is
Its context window, the most tokens it can process at once
Its embedding size, which the vector database sets for it
Its training cut-off, which fixes the latest date of its knowledge
1.why: The context window caps how many tokens of input and output a model can process at once. Long documents may need chunking or retrieval.

1.q: An AI malware detector catches 95% of malware, but raises so many false alarms that analysts have started ignoring it. Which metric needs improving?
o: Recall, since too much malware is still getting past the detector
Precision, since too many of its alerts turn out to be false positives
Latency, since alerts are reaching the analysts too slowly to act
Perplexity, since the detector’s language model is easily confused
1.why: Precision measures how many alerts are real. High recall with low precision floods analysts with false positives, leading to alert fatigue.

1.q: A demand forecasting model stays uncertain even after years more data are added, because customer behaviour is inherently random. Which type of uncertainty is this?
o: Epistemic uncertainty, which shrinks as more data is collected
Aleatoric uncertainty, which comes from randomness in the data
Model drift, which comes from changing deployment conditions
Calibration error, which comes from overconfident probabilities
1.why: Aleatoric uncertainty reflects irreducible randomness in the data. Epistemic uncertainty comes from limited knowledge, and more data can reduce it.

1.q: A summary of a security report adds a breach date that appears nowhere in the report and can’t be verified elsewhere. Which type of hallucination is this?
o: Intrinsic, because it contradicts a fact stated in the source
Extrinsic, because it adds content the source doesn’t support
A retrieval failure, because the report was missing from the index
Overfitting, because the model memorised other security reports
1.why: Extrinsic hallucinations add content the source doesn’t support; intrinsic ones contradict the source. Both call for grounding and verification.

1.q: A model reports 90% confidence on predictions that turn out to be right only 60% of the time. What does this show?
o: High precision, since most of its confident predictions are right
Poor calibration, since its certainty runs ahead of its accuracy
Concept drift, since the meaning of its labels has changed
Low recall, since it misses most of the cases it should find
1.why: A well-calibrated model that says 90% is right about 90% of the time. Overconfident scores mislead reviewers and automated decisions.

1.q: A team starting an AI project documents the system’s purpose, users, context and potential harms before measuring anything. Which NIST AI RMF function is this?
o: Govern, which sets culture, policies and accountability across functions
Map, which frames the system’s setting and identifies the risks in it
Measure, which analyses, assesses and tracks the identified risks
Manage, which prioritises the risks and decides how to act on them
1.why: Map establishes context and identifies risks. Measure assesses them, Manage treats them, and Govern is cross-cutting.

1.q: Under the EU AI Act, which risk tier MOST likely applies to an AI-based email spam filter?
o: Unacceptable risk, so the system is banned in the EU
Minimal risk, with no specific obligations under the Act
High risk, needing a conformity assessment before use
Limited risk, needing users to be told they face AI
1.why: Most AI, such as spam filters, is minimal risk with no specific obligations under the Act, although voluntary codes of conduct are encouraged.

1.q: The AI policy already requires approval for new AI tools, but staff keep asking how to get it, and each department follows a different process. Which document would BEST fix this?
o: A policy statement restating the organisation’s overall AI principles
A procedure setting out each step, its owner and the evidence required
A guideline offering optional tips for evaluating AI tools informally
A standard listing the encryption algorithms approved for AI services
1.why: The policy already sets the requirement; what is missing is the how. A procedure gives the step-by-step process, owners and evidence, so every department follows the same route. Guidelines are optional, and standards set specific mandatory technical requirements.

1.q: In the three lines model, which function provides independent assurance over AI risk management?
o: The first line, which owns and manages AI risks daily
The third line, internal audit, which reports to the board
The second line, which sets policy and oversees the risks
External vendors, who supply many of the AI models in use
1.why: Internal audit, the third line, gives independent assurance to the board. The first line owns risk, and the second line oversees it.

1.q: An organisation is forming an AI governance committee. Which membership is MOST appropriate?
o: Data scientists only, since they understand the models best
Business, legal, risk, privacy, security and technical leads
External vendors, since they supply most of the AI it uses
The marketing team, since it manages public perception of AI
1.why: AI risks cut across functions, so oversight needs business owners together with legal, risk, privacy, security and technical expertise.

1.q: A regulator asks whether a hiring tool selects applicants from each group at similar rates, regardless of qualifications. Which fairness metric is this?
o: Equal opportunity, which compares true positive rates across groups
Demographic parity, which compares selection rates across groups
Calibration, which compares how accurate the scores are by group
Individual fairness, which compares outcomes for similar people
1.why: Demographic parity compares selection rates across groups. Equal opportunity compares true positive rates among qualified people.

1.q: An organisation names a senior owner who must answer for each AI system’s outcomes and act on problems. Which principle does this MOST directly serve?
o: Transparency, telling people when and how AI is being used
Accountability, tying decisions to a responsible individual
Inclusiveness, making AI work well for diverse people
Robustness, keeping performance stable under stress
1.why: Accountability means identifiable people answer for AI outcomes and have the authority to act when problems arise.

1.q: Two fairness metrics give conflicting results for a loan model. Who should decide which metric the organisation uses?
o: The data scientist who built the model, as a purely technical decision
Accountable business and governance owners, as a documented policy choice
The model itself, by optimising for whichever metric is easiest to meet
The vendor of the fairness toolkit, through its default settings
1.why: Fairness metrics can conflict mathematically, so choosing one is a value judgement that accountable owners must make and document.

1.q: A risk committee wants to know which factors drive a credit model’s decisions across all applicants. Which kind of explanation fits BEST?
o: A counterfactual for one applicant who was recently declined
A global explanation of the model’s overall feature importance
The model’s raw weights, published for the committee to inspect
A local explanation of the most recent decision the model made
1.why: Global explanations describe overall model behaviour. Local explanations and counterfactuals explain individual decisions.

1.q: A model-theft incident would cost £800,000 and is expected once every eight years. What is its annualised loss expectancy?
o: £6,400,000, multiplying the loss by the eight years
£100,000, multiplying the single loss by an ARO of 0.125
£800,000, since the single loss applies in every year
£80,000, multiplying the single loss by an ARO of 0.1
1.why: ALE = SLE × ARO. Once every eight years gives an ARO of 0.125, so £800,000 × 0.125 = £100,000.

1.q: Which characteristic MOST increases the risk tier of an AI agent?
o: It uses a model with more parameters than the organisation’s other models
It can take irreversible actions on its own, such as making payments
It was built by an internal team rather than bought from a vendor
It can produce its answers in more than one language
1.why: Autonomy over irreversible, consequential actions raises impact and blast radius, which drives the risk tier.

1.q: After mitigation, an AI system’s residual risk is still above the organisation’s risk appetite. What should happen?
o: Launch anyway, and record the risk for review at next year’s audit
Apply further treatment, or avoid the risk, before the system launches
Lower the risk appetite, so that the residual risk falls within it
Ask the developers to accept the risk on the business’s behalf
1.why: Risk above appetite needs further treatment or avoidance. Accepting it requires an authorised owner and must fit the appetite; changing the appetite to fit is not treatment.

1.q: A retailer plans to train a model on years of customer purchase records to predict life events, such as pregnancy, for targeted offers. What should the privacy team require FIRST?
o: A penetration test of the model’s hosting environment before launch
A data protection impact assessment, before the processing begins
A customer survey about the targeted offers, run after launch
A model card describing the model’s accuracy for marketing sign-off
1.why: Profiling customers to infer sensitive life events is likely to be high-risk processing under the GDPR, so a DPIA is required before it starts. Testing and documentation come later and don’t replace the assessment.

1.q: Which details should each entry in an AI risk register include, so that the risk is actively managed?
o: Only the date on which the risk was first identified
The risk, its owner, rating, treatment and review date
The names of every person who uses the AI system
The model’s architecture and its total parameter count
1.why: A useful register entry names an owner, rates the risk, records the treatment decision and sets a review date, so accountability and follow-up are clear.

1.q: Developers use an AI coding assistant to write product code. Which practice BEST reduces the risk of shipping code that breaches open-source licences?
o: Ask the assistant to promise that its code is always original
Scan generated code for matches with licensed open-source code
Ban all open-source software from every one of the company’s products
Rely on the vendor’s marketing claims about its training data
1.why: Generated code can reproduce licensed snippets. Scanning outputs for matches, alongside review and vendor indemnities, manages the IP risk.

1.q: AI assistant chat logs are due for routine deletion, but legal counsel has issued a litigation hold that covers them. What should happen?
o: Delete them on schedule, since retention policy takes priority
Suspend deletion of all the relevant logs until the hold is lifted
Delete them early, before they can be requested in the litigation
Copy them to a personal drive, to keep them outside the system
1.why: A legal hold overrides routine deletion for the data it covers. Deleting held data can be unlawful; holds should be precise and released when they end.

1.q: An AI vendor offers to indemnify customers against copyright claims arising from its tool’s outputs. What should the customer check FIRST?
o: Nothing more, since an indemnity covers every possible claim
Its conditions, such as keeping the vendor’s filters switched on
Whether the vendor has more customers than its competitors
That it also covers any code that staff members write entirely by hand
1.why: Vendor IP indemnities often apply only if conditions are met, such as using built-in filters and not modifying outputs, so they must be read and followed.

1.q: A company keeps every prompt and response from its AI assistant indefinitely, “in case it is useful later”. Which principle does this MOST clearly breach?
o: Accuracy, which requires personal data to be kept up to date
Storage limitation, which limits retention to what is needed
Transparency, which requires telling people about processing
Integrity, which requires protection against unauthorised change
1.why: Retention needs a defined purpose and period. Keeping prompts indefinitely ‘just in case’ breaches storage limitation and enlarges the impact of any breach.

1.q: An AI vendor’s terms let it add new sub-processors at any time without telling customers. Why does this matter MOST?
o: Sub-processors always charge customers extra fees for each request
Customer data could flow to unvetted parties outside agreed controls
Adding new sub-processors automatically reduces the model’s accuracy
Sub-processors are banned from handling AI services in every country
1.why: Sub-processors handle customer data for the vendor. Customers need notice and a right to object, so data stays with vetted parties under agreed controls.

1.q: An AI vendor answers “yes” to every control in a security questionnaire. What should the assessor do next?
o: Accept the answers, since vendors are legally bound by them
Ask for evidence, such as audit reports, tests and policies
Reject the vendor, since perfect answers are always dishonest
Send the same questionnaire again in a month, to compare
1.why: Questionnaire answers are claims. Due diligence verifies them with evidence, such as independent audit reports, test results and policies, scoped to the service.

1.q: When should an organisation plan its exit from a critical AI vendor?
o: Only once the vendor formally announces that it is closing the service
At onboarding, with data return, certified deletion and transition
After the first major incident involving the vendor’s service
Never, since exit plans signal distrust and harm the relationship
1.why: Exit is planned from day one: data and models returned in usable form, deletion certified and a transition path agreed, so the organisation isn’t locked in.

1.q: An AI vendor passed a thorough due diligence review at onboarding. What should happen for the rest of the contract?
o: Nothing further, since the vendor has already been fully approved
Ongoing monitoring of model changes, incidents and service performance
A full repeat of the onboarding review every month, regardless of risk
Monitoring of the vendor’s invoices for unexpected price rises only
1.why: Vendor risk changes over time. Ongoing monitoring of model and sub-processor changes, incidents and performance keeps assurance current.

1.q: A supervisor pauses an agent’s batch of outgoing payments to adjust its settings, then lets it continue. Which decision authority is being used?
o: Override, replacing one of the AI’s outputs with a human decision
Intervention, steering a process while it is still running
Sign-off, giving formal approval at a release or change gate
Stop, halting the whole system immediately and safely
1.why: Intervention pauses, adjusts or redirects a running process. Override replaces a specific output, sign-off approves at gates, and stop halts the system.

1.q: A newsroom relies only on C2PA content credentials to spot AI-generated images sent in by the public. What is the main weakness?
o: C2PA credentials can only be read by the same camera that made them
Metadata is often stripped when images are copied or re-encoded
C2PA works only for text, and can’t describe images or video
Content credentials always reveal the photographer’s address
1.why: Provenance metadata is valuable but easily lost. A missing credential proves nothing, so combine it with watermark detection and other checks.

1.q: An external auditor has been asked to review an AI system. Which evidence is MOST useful?
o: Marketing material that describes the system’s benefits to customers
Model cards, impact assessments, decision logs and test results
A list of the developers’ names, job titles and qualifications
Screenshots of the system’s user interface during normal use
1.why: Audit relies on documented evidence of design, assessment, decisions and testing, not on marketing or appearance.

1.q: An organisation measures whether its AI awareness programme has reduced the number of AI-related data incidents. Which Kirkpatrick level is this?
o: Level 1, Reaction: how people felt about the training
Level 4, Results: the effect on the organisation’s outcomes
Level 2, Learning: what participants know after training
Level 3, Behaviour: whether people apply it in their work
1.why: Level 4 measures organisational results, such as fewer incidents. Level 3 measures behaviour change; levels 1 and 2 measure reaction and learning.

1.q: Finance staff could be targeted by deepfake voice calls requesting urgent payments. Which training approach is MOST effective?
o: An annual policy document that staff confirm they have read
Realistic simulations, with coaching and a clear verification step
A general lecture on how neural networks generate synthetic audio
A poster campaign reminding staff that AI is a powerful technology
1.why: Scenario-based simulations with immediate feedback and a clear verification procedure, such as a call-back, change behaviour more than passive content.

1.q: Three datasets are each harmless on their own, but a model trained on all of them can infer who individual people are. What is this called?
o: Label persistence, where classifications carry over into derived data
The mosaic effect, where combined data reveals what each part hides
Data localisation, where data must remain within national borders
Chain of custody, where each transfer of the data is recorded
1.why: The mosaic effect occurs when combining datasets reveals sensitive information that none reveals alone, so combined data may need a higher classification.

1.q: A dataset’s business owner decides who may use it and for what. Its backups have been failing for weeks, and nobody has acted. Who is MOST directly responsible for fixing the backups?
o: The data owner, who must personally carry out all technical work on it
The data custodian, who operates the storage and its technical controls
The data protection officer, who monitors compliance with privacy law
The data scientists, who are the main users of the training dataset
1.why: Custodians operate the storage, backups and technical controls on the owner’s behalf. The owner stays accountable and sets requirements but doesn’t run the systems, and the DPO advises and monitors.

1.q: A company hires a vendor to label customer images on its behalf, following its instructions. Which document should govern the vendor’s processing?
o: A non-disclosure agreement covering only the vendor’s staff
A data processing agreement setting purpose, security and limits
A public privacy notice published on the company’s main website
A service level agreement covering only labelling turnaround
1.why: A processor acting on the controller’s instructions needs a data processing agreement setting out purpose, instructions, security, sub-processors and deletion.

1.q: A UK bank requires its AI provider to store all customer data in UK data centres. The provider’s parent company is based abroad, under rules that let local authorities demand information held anywhere by its subsidiaries. Which concern does the residency requirement MOST clearly leave unaddressed?
o: Availability, since hosting in one country rules out any redundancy
Sovereignty, since another country’s laws may still apply to the data
Retention, since UK law requires all AI training data to be deleted yearly
Portability, since UK-hosted data can’t legally move to another provider
1.why: Residency controls where data sits; sovereignty concerns whose laws apply. A provider subject to foreign law may be compelled to hand over data it controls, wherever it is stored. Contracts, customer-held keys and sovereign cloud options address this.

1.q: An EU company wants an AI provider in a country without an adequacy decision to process its customers’ personal data. Which mechanism is commonly used?
o: A verbal assurance from the provider’s sales team that data is safe
Standard contractual clauses, with a transfer risk assessment
Encrypting the data with keys that the provider itself holds
A brief mention of the transfer in the company’s privacy notice
1.why: Transfers to countries without adequacy need a safeguard, typically standard contractual clauses, supported by a transfer risk assessment and any supplementary measures.

1.q: Before publishing a de-identified dataset, a UK organisation asks whether a determined person, without specialist skills, could re-identify anyone. What is this test called?
o: The k-anonymity check, counting identical records in each group
The motivated intruder test, a key benchmark for anonymisation
The membership inference test, run against a trained model
The minimum necessary standard, taken from US health law
1.why: The motivated intruder test asks whether a reasonably competent, determined person using available resources could re-identify individuals.

1.q: A mobile app needs usage statistics, but the company must never see users’ raw values. Which privacy technique fits BEST?
o: Central differential privacy, adding noise to results on the server
Local differential privacy, adding noise on each device before collection
Pseudonymisation, replacing user names with random IDs on the server
Encryption at rest, protecting the raw values once they are stored
1.why: Local differential privacy adds noise on the device, so the collector never receives true individual values. Central DP trusts the server with raw data.

1.q: An attacker who knows some of a person’s details uses a model’s outputs to deduce their health condition. What is this attack?
o: Membership inference, revealing whether a record was in training
Attribute inference, deducing a sensitive trait about a person
Model extraction, copying the model’s behaviour into a substitute
Data poisoning, corrupting the model through its training data
1.why: Attribute inference uses model outputs and known details to infer sensitive attributes. Membership inference reveals whether a record was in the training data.

1.q: A data scientist finds that a fraud model’s training extract includes card security codes (CVV2) copied from payment processing logs. What does PCI DSS require?
o: Keep them, as long as the training extract is encrypted at rest
Remove them, as they mustn’t be stored after authorisation
Keep them, as long as the card numbers are pseudonymised
Remove them only if model accuracy doesn’t depend on them
1.why: Sensitive authentication data, such as card security codes, must not be stored after authorisation, even if encrypted, so it can’t be used for training.

1.q: Which training approach limits each record’s influence to one part of the model, so that honouring a deletion request needs only that part to be retrained?
o: Federated learning, which trains across separate devices
SISA training, which isolates data into separate shards
Differential privacy, which adds noise during training
Transfer learning, which reuses a pre-trained model
1.why: SISA (sharded, isolated, sliced, aggregated) training limits each record’s influence to one shard, so removing it needs only that shard retrained.

1.q: Attackers add correctly labelled but subtly altered images to a training set, so that the model later misclassifies one target. Why won’t a review of labels catch this?
o: Label reviews only ever check a tiny random sample of the data
The labels are correct; the poison is in the content itself
Altered images are always removed by normal data augmentation
Image models don’t use labels at all during their training
1.why: Clean-label poisoning keeps labels correct and hides the attack in the content, so label checks miss it. Provenance and data validation are needed.

1.q: After a poisoning incident, investigators can’t tell whether approved training snapshots were altered, because administrators could edit them. Which control would BEST prevent this in future?
o: Weekly manual reviews of a random sample of the stored training files
Immutable write-once storage, with retention locks for a fixed period
Faster storage, so that snapshots can be recreated from source quickly
Longer passwords for the administrators who manage the storage system
1.why: Write-once (WORM) storage with retention locks stops anyone, including administrators, from changing or deleting approved snapshots for a set period, so their integrity can be trusted. Sampling, speed and passwords don’t give that guarantee.

1.q: A model scores 98% in testing, but many test records were also in its training data. What does this MOST likely mean?
o: The model is ready for production, since 98% beats any benchmark
Train–test leakage has inflated the score, overstating real performance
The test set is too small, but the overlap itself doesn’t matter
The model has underfitted, since it saw the test data beforehand
1.why: Train–test leakage lets a model be scored on data it has already seen, inflating results. Test sets must be kept strictly separate.

1.q: Two annotators label the same set of images and agree on only 55% of them. What does this MOST likely indicate?
o: Both annotators are deliberately poisoning the labels together
Unclear guidelines or unreliable labels, needing review first
The images are too high in resolution for annotators to judge
The labels are fine, since agreement is never above 60%
1.why: Low inter-annotator agreement suggests ambiguous guidelines, poor training or bad labels. Investigate before the data is used.

1.q: An attacker uses a face recognition model’s outputs to reconstruct a recognisable image of someone in its training data. What is this attack?
o: Membership inference, revealing if a face was in training
Model inversion, recovering likenesses of people it learned from
Evasion, altering a face so that the model misidentifies it
Model extraction, copying the model’s behaviour via queries
1.why: Model inversion reconstructs representative training data, such as faces, from a model’s outputs or confidence scores.

1.q: A genomics company stores encrypted training data that must stay confidential for at least 30 years. Which cryptographic action is MOST important to plan for?
o: Replacing AES-256, since quantum computers will break it outright
Migrating key establishment to post-quantum algorithms, such as ML-KEM
Compressing the data before encryption, so less of it can be harvested
Replacing encryption with hashing, since hashes can never be reversed
1.why: Data captured today could be decrypted later if its key exchange relies on RSA or elliptic curves, which large quantum computers could break. Moving to post-quantum key establishment such as ML-KEM (FIPS 203) protects long-lived data. AES-256 is still considered strong.

1.q: A bank’s DLP flags thousands of prompts a day because they contain any 16-digit number, and analysts can’t spot actual leaks among the false alarms. Which change BEST cuts the noise while still catching genuine leaks?
o: Turning off DLP for prompts, since AI tools already filter sensitive data
Exact data match, using fingerprints of the bank’s real customer records
Flagging only prompts that contain five or more 16-digit numbers
Blocking every prompt that contains any digits, whatever the context
1.why: Exact data match compares content against hashed fingerprints of the organisation’s actual records, so it flags real customer data rather than anything that looks like a card number. Disabling DLP, crude thresholds or blocking all digits are far worse trade-offs.

1.q: A cloud analytics service must run calculations on customer data without ever decrypting it. Which technique makes this possible?
o: Tokenisation, which swaps sensitive values for random tokens
Homomorphic encryption, which computes directly on ciphertext
Envelope encryption, which wraps data keys with a master key
Transport encryption, which protects data moving over networks
1.why: Homomorphic encryption lets computation happen on encrypted data, at a high performance cost. The other options protect data at rest, in transit or by substitution.

1.q: An AI support tool should show most staff only the last four digits of card numbers, without changing the stored data. Which technique fits?
o: Static masking, which permanently overwrites the stored values
Dynamic data masking, applied whenever the data is queried
Cryptographic erase, which destroys the encryption keys
Hashing, which replaces each value with a one-way digest
1.why: Dynamic data masking hides sensitive values at query time based on the user’s role, leaving stored data unchanged for authorised uses.

1.q: A credit model’s developers want to sign off its validation themselves, to meet a launch date. What is the BEST response from the model risk manager?
o: Accept their sign-off, since the developers understand the model best
Require validation by a qualified party independent of the build team
Skip validation for now, and validate at the first annual model review
Ask the developers to double the number of tests they run themselves
1.why: Independent validation provides effective challenge, free of the developers’ assumptions and incentives. It is a core principle of model risk management, as in SR 11-7. More self-testing doesn’t remove the conflict of interest.

1.q: How does a hash chain make an AI system’s audit log tamper-evident?
o: Each entry is encrypted with a different key held by the auditors
Each entry includes the previous entry’s hash, exposing later edits
The whole log is compressed into one file each night for storage
Entries are written by the model itself, so no one else can edit them
1.why: Linking each entry to the previous one’s hash means any change or deletion breaks every later link, making tampering detectable.

1.q: A document-drafting assistant returns Office files that staff open directly. Which control removes macros and other active content before files reach users?
o: Encryption, which stops unauthorised people from reading the files
Content disarm and reconstruction, rebuilding clean copies of files
Watermarking, which marks each file as having been made by the assistant
Compression, which reduces each file’s size before it is sent
1.why: Content disarm and reconstruction strips active elements, such as macros and scripts, and rebuilds files with only known-safe content.

1.q: A provider’s high-risk AI system, on the EU market for a year, has begun making more errors for one group of users. Which provider obligation under the AI Act is MOST directly meant to catch and act on this?
o: A fresh conformity assessment before anyone may keep using the system
Post-market monitoring, collecting and analysing performance in use
A fundamental rights impact assessment, carried out by the provider
Registration of the issue in an EU database of general-purpose models
1.why: Providers of high-risk systems must run a post-market monitoring system that collects and analyses data on performance in use, so emerging problems are found and corrected. Fundamental rights impact assessments fall to certain deployers, and general-purpose models are a separate regime.

1.q: What does keyless signing, as used by Sigstore, bind a model’s signature to?
o: A long-lived private key stored on the developer’s own laptop
A short-lived certificate for a verified identity, logged publicly
The model’s file size and the exact date when it was first uploaded
A shared password known to everyone in the model publishing team
1.why: Keyless signing issues short-lived certificates tied to an authenticated identity and records signatures in a public transparency log, avoiding long-lived keys.

1.q: A provider wants to detect whether text circulating online was generated by its own model. Which technique fits BEST?
o: A model watermark that responds to a secret set of trigger inputs
An output watermark embedded statistically in what it writes
A digital signature applied to the model’s weight files
A per-licensee fingerprint in each customer’s copy of the model
1.why: Output watermarks mark generated content itself, so text can be tested later. Model watermarks and fingerprints identify copies of the model, not its outputs.

1.q: A model passed integrity checks at the deployment gate. Weeks later, investigators find its file in storage was swapped, and the serving system ran the swapped file without noticing. Which control would BEST have prevented this?
o: Running the deployment gate checks more often, such as every night
Verifying the model’s signature again each time the file is loaded
Encrypting the storage volume that holds the model files at rest
Logging every model load, so that swaps can be found during audits
1.why: Verification at the gate only proves the file was good at that moment. Verifying the signature at load time catches files altered or swapped in storage afterwards. Nightly checks leave gaps, encryption at rest doesn’t stop tampering through authorised access, and logs only help after the fact.

1.q: A customer-facing AI API must allow short bursts, such as a user pasting several documents at once, while holding each user to a steady average rate. Which rate-limiting design fits BEST?
o: A fixed window that resets the count at the start of every minute
A token bucket that refills continuously, up to a maximum burst size
A hard limit of one request per second, with no allowance for bursts
A monthly quota, with no limit on how quickly requests can be made
1.why: A token bucket lets a client spend saved-up tokens in a burst, up to the bucket size, while the refill rate enforces the long-run average. Fixed windows allow double bursts at window edges, and quotas don’t control the rate.

1.q: Attackers edit public web pages just before a dataset’s scheduled snapshot is taken, then revert them. What is this attack?
o: Split-view poisoning, changing content after a URL list is curated
Frontrunning poisoning, exploiting predictable collection times
Typosquatting, registering names that look like popular ones
Dependency confusion, publishing a public package over a private one
1.why: Frontrunning poisoning times malicious edits to be captured in a periodic snapshot, then reverts them so reviewers see clean pages.

1.q: A developer’s general-purpose AI model was trained using more than 10²⁵ floating-point operations of compute. Under the EU AI Act, what MOST likely follows?
o: The model is automatically banned from being offered in the EU market
It is presumed to pose systemic risk, adding duties such as adversarial testing
It must be registered as a high-risk AI system under Annex III of the Act
It is exempt from transparency duties because of its scale and capability
1.why: Training compute above 10²⁵ FLOPs creates a presumption of high-impact capabilities, so the model is treated as a general-purpose AI model with systemic risk. Its provider must evaluate and adversarially test it, assess and mitigate systemic risks, report serious incidents and ensure cyber security.

1.q: A data scientist installs a package named “pytorch-utilz”, mistyping a popular library’s name, and it steals cloud credentials. What attack is this?
o: Dependency confusion, preferring a public package over a private one
Typosquatting, registering look-alike names to catch slips
Model namespace reuse, re-registering a deleted publisher’s name
Frontrunning, timing malicious edits to a dataset snapshot
1.why: Typosquatting relies on look-alike names catching typing mistakes. Pinned, allow-listed dependencies from internal mirrors reduce the risk.

1.q: A model hub shows a “verified publisher” badge on a model’s page. What does this badge tell you?
o: The model has been scanned and found free of any backdoors
The account belongs to the organisation it claims to be
The hub guarantees the model’s accuracy for every use case
The model’s licence permits any commercial use at all
1.why: Verification confirms the publisher’s identity, not the model’s safety. Pin revisions, scan files and evaluate the model before use.

1.q: An internal RAG assistant trusts any request from inside the corporate network, and any document already in its index. Which change BEST applies Zero Trust principles?
o: Moving the assistant into its own network segment, then trusting it fully
Verifying every user and request, and treating indexed content as untrusted
Adding a stronger firewall at the network perimeter around the assistant
Requiring a VPN connection, so that only internal users can reach it
1.why: Zero Trust removes implicit trust based on network location: every identity and request is verified, access is least privilege, and content the model reads is treated as untrusted. Segments, firewalls and VPNs alone still rely on location.

1.q: An assistant fetches order details through an API that checks the user is signed in, but not that the order belongs to them. Which weakness is this?
o: Token passthrough, forwarding the client’s token to downstream APIs
Missing object-level authorisation on each requested record
Tool poisoning, hiding instructions in a tool’s description
A rug pull, where a tool’s behaviour changes after approval
1.why: Object-level authorisation checks that the caller may access the specific record requested. Without it, any signed-in user can fetch others’ data by changing an ID.

1.q: Which control MOST directly limits an attacker’s lateral movement from a compromised inference server to the training data stores?
o: Longer and more complex passwords for every data science user
Micro-segmentation, with tightly controlled traffic between zones
A larger model, which is assumed to resist attacks more strongly
Annual penetration tests of the organisation’s external perimeter
1.why: Micro-segmentation divides workloads into small zones with deny-by-default traffic rules, so one compromised server can’t freely reach others.

1.q: A team begins a STRIDE threat model of a new RAG assistant. Which artefact should it usually create first?
o: A marketing plan describing how and when the assistant will be launched
A data flow diagram of components, stores, flows and boundaries
A list of every possible prompt that users might send to it
The final penetration test report from the previous system
1.why: Threat modelling starts from a data flow diagram showing components, data stores, external entities, flows and trust boundaries, to which STRIDE is applied.

1.q: An architecture decision record documents why a team chose not to log full prompts. What is its MAIN value?
o: It replaces the need for any privacy impact assessment
It records the reasoning and residual risk for later review
It guarantees that the decision complies with every law
It lets the team change the decision without any approval
1.why: ADRs capture context, options, reasoning and residual risk, so decisions can be reviewed and revisited when circumstances change.

1.q: An assessment finds that the baseboard management controllers (BMCs) on GPU training servers are reachable from the office network and still use default passwords. What should be done FIRST?
o: Change the default passwords at the next annual maintenance window
Move them to an isolated management network and change the passwords
Block the office network’s internet access to protect the controllers
Encrypt the training data that is stored on the servers’ local disks
1.why: BMCs give out-of-band control below the operating system, so exposure with default credentials allows a full takeover of the hardware. Isolating them on a restricted management network and replacing the credentials is the urgent fix; firmware updates follow.

1.q: Which Kubernetes baseline stops containers on an inference cluster from running privileged or as root?
o: Horizontal pod autoscaling, set with a maximum replica count
Pod Security Standards, enforced at the restricted level
Resource quotas that cap the GPUs each namespace may use
Node affinity rules that pin pods to particular GPU types
1.why: Pod Security Standards define baseline and restricted profiles that block privileged containers, root users and host access.

1.q: A cloud GPU cluster’s bill spikes, and its GPUs show full utilisation even though no jobs are scheduled. What is the MOST likely cause?
o: A routine driver update that runs on every GPU each month
Cryptojacking, with attackers using the GPUs to mine currency
Model drift, which makes inference far more expensive over time
A logging misconfiguration that inflates the reported usage
1.why: Unexplained full GPU utilisation and cost spikes suggest hijacked compute, as in the ShadowRay campaign. Investigate exposed dashboards and credentials.

1.q: During extreme demand, an inference service drops low-priority batch requests to keep customer-facing responses within target. What is this called?
o: Autoscaling, which adds capacity automatically as demand rises
Load shedding, sacrificing less important work under pressure
Preemption, which evicts running jobs to make way for others
Rate limiting, which caps how often each client may send requests
1.why: Load shedding deliberately drops or defers low-priority work under pressure, so that critical services keep meeting their targets.

1.q: Model builds run on long-lived CI runners that are reused across projects. After one build ran a malicious dependency, the team fears later builds were tampered with. Which change BEST prevents this kind of persistence?
o: Scanning every runner for malware once a month, then cleaning it
Using a fresh, ephemeral runner for each build, destroyed afterwards
Giving each project’s runner a longer and stronger admin password
Running builds only at night, when fewer engineers are working
1.why: Ephemeral runners start clean for every job and are destroyed afterwards, so anything an attacker plants can’t persist into later builds. Periodic scans and passwords don’t stop a compromised runner contaminating the next job.

1.q: Why are distroless images often preferred for model-serving containers?
o: They run models faster by compiling them directly into the kernel
They omit shells and package managers, shrinking the attack surface
They encrypt the model weights automatically while serving
They allow any package to be installed at runtime when needed
1.why: Distroless images contain only the application and its runtime dependencies, leaving attackers fewer tools and fewer vulnerable packages.

1.q: A training pipeline breaks whenever an upstream team renames fields in a data feed. Which practice BEST prevents this?
o: Allowing the pipeline to guess the meaning of any new field names
A data contract agreeing the feed’s schema, quality and ownership
Copying the upstream team’s database into the pipeline each night
Turning off schema validation so that the pipeline never fails
1.why: A data contract sets out a feed’s schema, quality rules, meaning and ownership, so changes are agreed and checked rather than silently breaking consumers.

1.q: An AI release pipeline checks that each model passes its safety evaluation suite. A failure would expose customers to harmful outputs. Which configuration is BEST for this check?
o: A soft gate that warns the team but lets the release continue
A hard gate that blocks the release until the failure is resolved
A dashboard metric that is reviewed at the end of each quarter
An optional check that teams may run when they have spare time
1.why: Checks whose failure would cause unacceptable harm should be hard gates that block release. Soft gates, which warn and need sign-off to proceed, suit lower-risk checks where a documented override is acceptable.

1.q: Which statement about prompt injection guardrails is MOST accurate?
o: A good enough classifier can stop every single injection attempt
No guardrail stops every injection, so limit what outputs can do
Guardrails are unnecessary if the system prompt is kept secret
Injection only affects models that were trained on public data
1.why: Injection can’t be filtered out completely, so systems must limit the consequences: least privilege, approvals and output validation.

1.q: A model is trained to give system and developer instructions priority over user input, and user input priority over tool content. What is this?
o: Context budgeting, which reserves context space for key instructions
An instruction hierarchy, which ranks sources when they conflict
Spotlighting, which marks untrusted content in the prompt
Plan-then-execute, which fixes the plan before reading data
1.why: An instruction hierarchy trains models to prefer higher-privilege instructions when sources conflict. It helps, but doesn’t guarantee resistance to injection.

1.q: A team deliberately cuts off its AI service’s model provider in a controlled test, to check that the fallbacks work. What is this practice?
o: Load testing, which measures performance under expected traffic
Chaos engineering, which injects failures to test resilience
Fuzzing, which sends malformed inputs to find crashes
Soak testing, which runs the service for long periods
1.why: Chaos engineering deliberately injects failures, such as a provider outage, to test a hypothesis about how the system behaves and recovers.

1.q: Which testing technique feeds an AI application large numbers of random or malformed inputs to uncover crashes and unsafe behaviour?
o: Soak testing, which runs a steady load for many hours
Fuzzing, which hunts for edge-case failures automatically
Spike testing, which applies sudden bursts of traffic
Regression testing, which repeats known test cases
1.why: Fuzzing generates random or structured input variations to find crashes, parsing errors and unsafe behaviour that normal tests miss.

1.q: Before an assistant lets a user approve a large payment, it asks them to re-authenticate with a passkey. What is this control?
o: Single sign-on, which signs users in once for many applications
Step-up authentication, requiring stronger proof for risky actions
SCIM provisioning, which creates and removes accounts automatically
Session time-out, which signs users out after a period of inactivity
1.why: Step-up authentication asks for fresh, stronger authentication before sensitive actions, limiting the damage from a hijacked session.

1.q: A vault issues an agent a database credential for one task, then revokes it automatically when the task ends. What is this?
o: A static secret, rotated manually by an administrator each year
A dynamic secret, created just in time and short-lived by design
A shared secret, used by every agent that connects to the database
A hard-coded secret, compiled into the agent’s container image
1.why: Dynamic secrets are generated on demand for one task or session and revoked afterwards, so a stolen credential has little lasting value.

1.q: Engineers sometimes sign in to the company’s AI platform from personal, unmanaged laptops in public places. Which identity control BEST limits this risk without blocking legitimate work?
o: Banning all remote access to the AI platform for every engineer
Conditional access, requiring a compliant device and assessing context
A signed policy in which engineers promise to use managed devices
Doubling the minimum password length for all platform accounts
1.why: Conditional access evaluates signals such as device compliance, location and risk at sign-in, and can require a managed device or step-up authentication. A ban stops legitimate work, and promises or passwords don’t enforce anything about the device.

1.q: An attacker with a stolen password sends an ML engineer repeated sign-in push prompts until one is approved. What is this, and the BEST defence?
o: Credential stuffing, defended by longer and more complex passwords
MFA fatigue, defended by phishing-resistant methods such as passkeys
Password spraying, defended by locking every account after one failure
Session hijacking, defended by shorter session cookie lifetimes
1.why: MFA fatigue floods users with push requests. Phishing-resistant methods, such as passkeys, remove the one-tap approval that it exploits.

1.q: An agent can read the full customer database and also send email to any external address. Each permission was approved separately. What risk do these permissions create together?
o: Excessive autonomy, since the agent acts without human approval
A toxic combination, letting one identity complete data theft alone
Configuration drift, since its permissions changed without review
A rug pull, since its tools changed behaviour after approval
1.why: Permissions that are acceptable alone can together let one identity complete a sensitive process, here reading and exfiltrating data. Review combinations, not just items.

1.q: An agent should read contract files only during business hours, only for its user’s own region, and never files labelled “restricted”. Which access control model fits these rules BEST?
o: Role-based access control, giving the agent a single “contracts” role
Attribute-based access control, evaluating time, location and labels
Discretionary access control, letting each file’s owner decide ad hoc
Mandatory access control, based only on government clearance levels
1.why: Attribute-based access control decides using attributes of the subject, resource, action and environment, such as time, region and sensitivity labels. A single role can’t express these conditions without an explosion of roles.

1.q: An agent’s tool calls are authorised once when its task starts, and never checked again. Which principle does this violate?
o: Defence in depth, which layers several independent controls
Complete mediation, which leaves no access request unverified
Secure by default, which ships with risky features turned off
Separation of duties, which splits sensitive tasks between people
1.why: Complete mediation requires every access to be checked in downstream systems, not just once, so changes in context or permission take effect.

1.q: An agent only needs to read calendar availability, but its calendar plugin can also create, edit and delete events. Which weakness is this?
o: Excessive autonomy, as the agent acts without any human review
Excessive functionality, as the plugin exposes surplus operations
Excessive permissions, as the agent’s identity has administrator rights
Excessive cost, as the plugin uses too many tokens per request
1.why: Excessive functionality means tools offer more operations than the task needs (OWASP LLM06). Use narrow tools that expose only what is required.

1.q: An agent starts an eight-hour data migration on behalf of an employee. Two hours in, the employee is dismissed and their account is disabled. Which authorisation design BEST handles this?
o: The agent finishes the task, since it was authorised when it started
Access is re-evaluated during the task, so the agent’s rights end too
The agent continues, and its logs are reviewed at the end of the month
The task pauses until the employee confirms they still want it to run
1.why: Authority delegated by a user should end when the user’s own access ends. Continuous evaluation, for example with short-lived tokens and revocation signals, stops the agent acting on a dismissed employee’s behalf.

1.q: Every new ML engineer automatically receives write access to all training datasets on their first day. What is the MAIN risk?
o: New engineers can’t start work until each dataset is approved
Over-broad birthright access gives people more than they need
Datasets become corrupted when too many people can read them
Automatic access breaks the joiner process in most HR systems
1.why: Birthright access should be the minimum common to a role. Broad default write access spreads excess privilege and widens insider and compromise risk.

1.q: A cloud estate has hundreds of AI workload identities, and nobody knows which of their permissions are actually used. Which tool would BEST support right-sizing them?
o: A cloud web application firewall in front of the AI services
A cloud infrastructure entitlement management (CIEM) platform
A cloud vulnerability scanner for the workloads’ containers
A data loss prevention policy for the workloads’ buckets
1.why: CIEM tools calculate the effective permissions of cloud identities, including workloads, and highlight permissions that are never used, so they can be removed. Firewalls, scanners and DLP address different problems.

1.q: Which capability detects and responds in real time to attacks on identities themselves, such as stolen agent tokens being replayed?
o: Data security posture management, which finds and classifies stored data
Identity threat detection and response, a specialist SOC capability
Content moderation, which screens model outputs for harm
Vulnerability scanning, which finds missing software patches
1.why: ITDR monitors identity systems and token use for attacks such as token theft, replay and privilege escalation, and responds in real time.

1.q: An engineer edits a guardrail setting directly on a production server. Within minutes, the setting reverts to the version stored in the repository. Which practice did this?
o: Load shedding, which drops low-priority work under heavy demand
GitOps reconciliation, restoring the approved state from Git
Model drift detection, which compares inputs with a baseline
A circuit breaker, which trips when error rates exceed a threshold
1.why: GitOps reconciliation continuously compares the running system with the desired state in version control, restoring or flagging unapproved changes.

1.q: An incident team carries out its real containment procedures for a poisoned model in a test environment, rather than just discussing them. Which exercise is this?
o: A tabletop exercise, in which participants talk through a scenario
A functional exercise, a realistic hands-on rehearsal of the response
A post-implementation review, held after an emergency change
A red team exercise, in which testers attack the live system
1.why: Functional exercises have participants perform real procedures in a test environment. Tabletop exercises discuss responses without carrying them out.

1.q: A team suspects that settings on its production AI gateway have drifted, but different engineers remember different “correct” values. What should it establish FIRST?
o: A rota of engineers who check the settings by hand every morning
An approved, version-controlled baseline to measure drift against
A new gateway product that has fewer configurable settings to manage
An all-staff email asking everyone not to change any settings
1.why: Drift can only be detected against a known, approved baseline of settings and versions. Once the baseline is under version control, tools can compare against it continuously and reconcile changes.

1.q: A model’s accuracy has been falling for weeks. Its accountable business owner says monitoring and retraining aren’t their job. Who is MOST appropriately responsible for this day-to-day work?
o: The internal audit team, which reviews models on an annual cycle
The model’s technical owner, who looks after its health in production
The vendor that supplied the base model the system was built on
The data protection officer, who oversees personal data processing
1.why: The model owner stays accountable, while a technical owner looks after its day-to-day health: monitoring, fixes and retraining. Audit gives independent assurance, and the DPO advises on data protection.

1.q: A SOC receives AI events from a gateway, an agent framework and a model provider, each in a different format. Which practice makes them easier to query together?
o: Storing each source’s events in a separate, unlinked archive
Normalising them to a common schema, such as OCSF, on arrival
Converting every event into a free-text summary for analysts
Deleting fields that don’t appear in all three of the formats
1.why: Normalising events to a vendor-neutral schema, such as OCSF, lets detections and queries work consistently across sources.

1.q: Downstream fraud tools reject masked account numbers unless they still look like 16-digit numbers, and authorised staff must be able to recover the originals. Which technique fits?
o: Redaction, which replaces each value with a fixed placeholder
Format-preserving encryption, reversible with the right key
Generalisation, which replaces values with broader ranges
Unkeyed hashing, which turns values into fixed-length digests
1.why: Format-preserving encryption keeps the original format, so downstream tools still work, and authorised key holders can decrypt the values.

1.q: During an investigation, an agent’s tool calls appear to happen before the prompts that triggered them. What is the MOST likely cause?
o: The agent predicted the prompts before users actually sent them
Clock skew between the systems that recorded the events
Log injection, inserting fake entries into the agent’s logs
Embedding drift, shifting the agent’s inputs over time
1.why: Clock differences between systems distort the order of events. Synchronised time and UTC timestamps prevent misleading timelines.

1.q: An incident review finds that an agent platform’s logs stopped reaching the SIEM two days before the attack, and nobody noticed. Which control would BEST have revealed the problem in time?
o: A larger SIEM licence, so that more events can be stored for longer
Alerts on missing heartbeats and on gaps in log sequence numbers
A monthly report of the total events received from each source
Encrypting the log stream between the agent platform and the SIEM
1.why: Heartbeats and sequence numbers let the SIEM alert as soon as a source goes quiet or events go missing. A monthly report would be far too slow, and storage and encryption don’t detect silence.

1.q: A security team plants a decoy API key in an agent’s configuration files. The key has no legitimate use. What is its purpose?
o: To give the agent a spare key if its normal credential expires
To raise an alert if anyone ever uses it, signalling compromise
To reduce the provider’s bill by spreading usage across two keys
To test whether the agent can rotate its own credentials safely
1.why: A honeytoken has no legitimate use, so any attempt to use it signals that someone has reached places they shouldn’t.

1.q: An engineer’s token is used to call the model registry from London and, ten minutes later, from Singapore. What does this signal suggest?
o: A normal pattern for engineers who travel often for their work
Impossible travel, a strong sign of stolen and reused credentials
A load balancer routing traffic through different cloud regions
Clock skew between the registry’s servers in the two regions
1.why: Use of one identity from places too far apart for the time between them suggests credential or token theft, needing investigation and revocation.

1.q: Attackers encode injected instructions in Base64 and unusual Unicode characters to slip them past an AI gateway’s filters. Which detection improvement helps MOST?
o: Scanning only inputs that are written in plain English text
Normalising and decoding inputs before they are scanned
Raising the model’s temperature to disrupt encoded commands
Blocking every request that contains any number at all
1.why: Input obfuscation hides malicious content in encodings and look-alike characters. Normalise and decode inputs before scanning them.

1.q: When an agent is approved, its permitted tools, data and actions are recorded. How does this record help detection later?
o: It lets the agent approve its own new permissions as needed
It acts as a purpose profile, a baseline for spotting misuse
It replaces the need to log the agent’s tool calls at all
It guarantees that the agent can never be manipulated
1.why: A purpose profile records the approved tools, data and actions, so activity outside it, such as a new tool or data source, stands out as possible misuse.

1.q: A secret scanner finds 400 possible credentials in old repositories, including API keys for model providers. The team can’t rotate them all at once. What should it do FIRST?
o: Rotate the credentials in alphabetical order of repository name
Check which credentials are still live, and rotate those ones first
Delete the old repositories, which removes the need to rotate any
Wait for providers to report misuse before rotating any of them
1.why: Validating which secrets are still active focuses effort on real exposure. Deleting repositories doesn’t revoke credentials that may already have been copied, and waiting for misuse is too late.

1.q: Which vulnerability prioritisation method uses a decision tree of exploitation status, exposure and impact, ending in outcomes such as “track” or “act”?
o: CVSS, which calculates a numeric base severity score
SSVC, Stakeholder-Specific Vulnerability Categorization
EPSS, which estimates the probability of exploitation
KEV, which lists vulnerabilities known to be exploited
1.why: SSVC (Stakeholder-Specific Vulnerability Categorization) walks a decision tree to reach track, track*, attend or act, reflecting context.

1.q: Which open resource catalogues AI failure modes and vulnerabilities, such as model behaviours, rather than only software flaws?
o: The National Vulnerability Database’s list of software CVE entries
AVID, a community-run database focused on AI-specific problems
The CIS Benchmarks for hardening operating systems and clouds
The OWASP Top 10 list of the most critical web application risks
1.why: AVID is an open knowledge base of AI failure modes and vulnerabilities, complementing CVE-based databases for software flaws.

1.q: A medium-severity flaw on an internal chatbot lets an attacker reach an over-privileged service account with access to customer data. Why does this raise its priority?
o: Internal chatbots are always the systems that attackers target first
It forms an attack path from the flaw through to sensitive data
Medium-severity flaws are automatically upgraded after 30 days
Service accounts are excluded from vulnerability management
1.why: Weaknesses that chain into an attack path to critical assets deserve higher priority than their individual scores suggest.

1.q: Which assessment ranks how critical each AI-supported activity is, based on the consequences of disrupting it, to guide vulnerability priorities and recovery targets?
o: A penetration test of the organisation’s external network
A business impact analysis, completed with process owners
A code review of the application that hosts each model
A user satisfaction survey covering all of the AI tools in use
1.why: A business impact analysis assesses the consequences of disrupting each process, ranking criticality for prioritisation and continuity planning.

1.q: An AI incident team lists its response options in order, from tightening guardrails through throttling to taking the system offline. What is this called?
o: A risk register, which records risks with owners and ratings
A containment ladder, choosing the lightest effective action
A kill chain, which models the stages of an attack
A RACI matrix, which assigns roles for each activity
1.why: A containment ladder orders options from least to most disruptive, so responders can choose the lightest action that stops the harm.

1.q: An AI chatbot is revealing other customers’ data in its answers. Which containment step is MOST appropriate FIRST?
o: Retrain the model on a cleaned dataset over the coming month
Restrict the feature or take it offline, while preserving evidence
Post an apology on social media before investigating further
Wait for more customers to report the problem to confirm it
1.why: Active data exposure needs immediate containment, with evidence preserved for investigation and notification decisions.

1.q: During an AI incident, responders collected logs, model files and prompts, but later can’t show who collected each item, when, or that it is unchanged. Which record would BEST have prevented this?
o: A daily status email summarising the progress of the investigation
An evidence manifest with source, collector, time, hash and location
A copy of the incident response plan, stored alongside the evidence
Screenshots of each system, taken at the end of the investigation
1.why: An evidence manifest records each preserved item with its source, collector, time, hash and storage location, supporting the chain of custody and the integrity of the evidence.

1.q: An AI incident has just been declared. Routine jobs will delete older prompt logs and superseded model versions overnight. What should responders do FIRST?
o: Let the jobs run, since only older data is going to be removed
Apply retention locks, so evidence isn’t deleted mid-investigation
Turn off all logging, so new records don’t overwrite the older ones
Ask the vendor to keep a copy of anything that it happens to hold
1.why: Preserving evidence comes before routine housekeeping. Retention locks or legal holds suspend deletion of logs, datasets and model versions the investigation may need. Turning off logging would lose future evidence.

1.q: A hijacked agent changed delivery addresses on 300 customer orders before it was stopped. Which step BEST deals with the changes already made?
o: Leave the changes in place, since the agent has now been stopped
Compensating transactions that restore the verified previous values
Delete the 300 orders, so that customers can place them again
Retrain the agent, so that it reverses the changes on its own
1.why: Compensating transactions reverse the effects of earlier actions, such as restoring records, using verified previous values and proper approval.

1.q: Which intrusion analysis model links four features of each event: adversary, capability, infrastructure and victim?
o: The Cyber Kill Chain, which orders the stages of an intrusion
The Diamond Model, used to pivot between related intrusions
STRIDE, which classifies threats into six distinct categories
The five whys, which drills down to an underlying cause
1.why: The Diamond Model links adversary, capability, infrastructure and victim, helping analysts pivot between related activity.

1.q: During root cause analysis, a team keeps asking why each failure happened until it reaches a cause that, if fixed, would prevent recurrence. Which technique is this?
o: A fishbone diagram, which groups causes into broad categories
The five whys, an iterative questioning method for root causes
Dataset diffing, which compares versions of a training dataset
Influence analysis, which links model behaviour to training data
1.why: The five whys technique repeats the question until it reaches a root cause whose fix would prevent recurrence.

1.q: Investigators suspect that poisoned records entered a training dataset between two versions. Which technique MOST directly finds them?
o: Rerunning the model on the same prompts used during the incident
Dataset diffing, comparing the before and after datasets
Raising the model’s temperature to expose hidden behaviour
Reviewing the model card for any mention of the dataset
1.why: Dataset diffing compares versions to find records that were added, removed or altered, narrowing the search for poisoned data.

1.q: An agent forwarded confidential files after reading an email containing hidden instructions. The team has disabled the agent’s email tool. Which further step is MOST important to stop the attack recurring?
o: Retrain the underlying model on a larger and more recent dataset
Find and remove the carrier message, and any copies of it elsewhere
Reset every employee’s password across the whole organisation
Share the attacker’s instructions widely so staff can recognise them
1.why: In indirect injection, the carrier is the content that delivered the instructions. Until every copy is found and removed, including indexed or cached copies, any assistant that reads it could be compromised again. Retraining and mass password resets don’t remove it.

1.q: A claims process can tolerate at most eight hours of disruption. Its AI triage service must be restored and then checked before claims can flow again. How should the service’s recovery time objective BEST be set?
o: At exactly eight hours, to match the maximum tolerable downtime
Well under eight hours, leaving time for checks and dependent steps
At twelve hours, since some manual processing would continue anyway
At twenty-four hours, in line with the provider’s standard SLA
1.why: The RTO must be shorter than the maximum tolerable downtime, leaving room for validation and any dependent steps before the business process resumes. Matching it exactly leaves no margin at all.

1.q: After restoring a vector store from a snapshot, which check BEST confirms that retrieval works as expected before it returns to production?
o: Checking that the database service starts without errors
Running golden queries that have known correct results
Asking a few users whether its answers seem better
Comparing the store’s size with the size before restore
1.why: Golden queries have known correct results, so they verify that a restored or changed index returns the right content.

1.q: An organisation wants to publish lessons from an AI incident so that anyone may share them freely. Which Traffic Light Protocol label applies?
o: TLP:RED, limited to the people present when it is shared
TLP:CLEAR, which sets no limits on any further disclosure
TLP:AMBER, shared within recipients’ organisations as needed
TLP:GREEN, shared within the recipients’ wider community
1.why: TLP:CLEAR means the information may be shared without restriction. RED, AMBER and GREEN progressively limit who may receive it.

1.q: A circuit breaker on an AI service trips because harmful outputs exceed a threshold. What happens next?
o: The service keeps serving harmful outputs until a person decides
Traffic moves to a safe fallback, then recovers via a half-open state
The model is permanently deleted, and then has to be rebuilt from scratch
All users are signed out at once, and their accounts are disabled
1.why: A tripped breaker routes traffic to a fallback, then tests recovery in a half-open state before fully restoring service.

1.q: A team must threat model a health assistant for risks such as users being linked across sessions or identified from their data. Which method fits BEST?
o: STRIDE, which focuses on six categories of security threats
LINDDUN, a method designed for privacy threat modelling
DREAD, which scores threats against five rating factors
PASTA, which links threats to business impact in stages
1.why: LINDDUN covers privacy threats: linking, identifying, non-repudiation, detecting, data disclosure, unawareness and non-compliance.

1.q: Attackers craft adversarial inputs against their own open-source copy of a similar model, then use them successfully against a company’s private model. What is this?
o: A white-box attack, using the target’s own weights directly
A transfer attack, exploiting similarities between models
A membership inference attack, revealing training records
A sponge attack, maximising the target model’s computation
1.why: Transfer attacks develop adversarial inputs on a proxy model and reuse them against a different target, so hiding a model’s weights isn’t a complete defence.

1.q: Attackers publish authoritative-looking pages so that a research assistant cites them as sources for false claims. What is this threat called?
o: Typosquatting, registering look-alike names for popular packages
Citation spoofing, a growing form of retrieval manipulation
Model inversion, reconstructing training data from outputs
Context stuffing, filling requests to drive up cost and latency
1.why: Citation spoofing plants sources that give false authority to an AI system’s answers. Source allow-lists and verification reduce the risk.

1.q: A threat modeller breaks the goal “steal the model’s weights” into the alternative steps and sub-goals that could achieve it. Which technique is this?
o: A data flow diagram, showing components, flows and stores
An attack tree, with the attacker’s objective at its root
A risk register, recording owners, ratings and treatments
A RACI matrix, assigning roles for each decision
1.why: Attack trees decompose an attacker’s goal into alternative sub-goals and steps, showing which paths are cheapest or least defended.

1.q: An insider who knows a model’s architecture and has its weights crafts adversarial inputs using its gradients. What type of attack is this?
o: A black-box attack, using only the model’s public outputs
A white-box attack, using full knowledge of the model
A transfer attack, using a different proxy model
A denial-of-wallet attack, driving up compute costs
1.why: White-box attacks use knowledge of the architecture and weights, such as gradients, making them the strongest form of adversarial attack.

1.q: A team keeps its AI system’s threat model in versioned, machine-readable files that are updated and reviewed with each design change. What is this practice?
o: Security through obscurity, hiding the design from attackers
Threat modelling as code, using tools such as pytm or Threagile
