Penetration testing, attacking the live system to find flaws
Configuration drift, where settings change outside control
1.why: Threat modelling as code describes systems and threats in versioned files, using tools such as Threat Dragon, pytm or Threagile, so models stay current.

1.q: A new assistant version goes first to internal staff, then to pilot customers, and finally to everyone. Which rollout strategy is this?
o: A big-bang release, switching all users at the same moment
A ring deployment, widening the audience in planned stages
A shadow deployment, where users never see new outputs
A blue/green switch, moving all traffic between two stacks
1.why: Ring deployments release to progressively wider groups, limiting exposure while confidence grows.

1.q: A newly released summarisation capability starts producing harmful output for a subset of users. The team must stop it within minutes, without a full redeployment. Which mechanism BEST supports this?
o: A scheduled release train, with the next deployment due in two weeks
A feature flag that can turn it off for some or all users at once
A code review of the change, before it goes into the next release
A user survey asking how often people use the new summaries
1.why: Feature flags separate release from deployment, so a capability can be switched off instantly for some or all users. Release trains and reviews take far longer and don’t stop current harm.

1.q: A release migrates a vector store to a new schema. Why should the migration be designed for backward compatibility?
o: So that the new schema runs faster than the previous one did
So that rolling back doesn’t break or corrupt the system’s data
So that the vendor can support the old version indefinitely
So that every user sees the change at exactly the same time
1.why: Backward-compatible changes let the previous release be restored without breaking or corrupting data, keeping rollback a real option.

1.q: Which 2025 ETSI technical specification sets baseline cyber security requirements for AI models and systems across their lifecycle?
o: ISO/IEC 27001, which certifies information security management
ETSI TS 104 223, derived from the UK’s AI code of practice
NIST SP 800-53, which catalogues US federal security controls
PCI DSS, which secures payment card data in organisations
1.why: ETSI TS 104 223 sets baseline cyber security requirements for AI models and systems, building on the UK’s AI Cyber Security Code of Practice.

1.q: An AI writing tool’s vendor sends customer text to a foundation model provider that the customer has no contract with. What is this risk called?
o: Concentration risk, from many services relying on one provider
Fourth-party risk, arising further down the supply chain
Model drift, from changes in the input data over time
Insider risk, from the customer’s own employees
1.why: Fourth-party risk comes from your vendors’ suppliers. Assess it through the vendor’s contracts, sub-processor lists and assurance reports.

1.q: Which MLCommons format provides machine-readable descriptions of machine learning datasets?
o: CycloneDX, a bill of materials standard from OWASP
Croissant, which can also record responsible AI details
Safetensors, a format for storing model weights safely
C2PA, a provenance standard for images and other media
1.why: Croissant is MLCommons’ machine-readable dataset metadata format, with responsible AI fields that support provenance and documentation.

1.q: A team wants to use an open model released under a Responsible AI Licence (OpenRAIL-M) in a product for its customers. What should the legal review check MOST carefully?
o: Whether the model’s weights may be stored on the company’s own servers
That its use-based restrictions are respected and passed on to users
Whether the licence permits the model to be fine-tuned in any way
That the model was trained on a dataset above a minimum size
1.why: RAIL licences allow broad use but prohibit specified uses, and require those restrictions to be passed on in derivative works and to downstream users. That is what distinguishes them from permissive licences such as Apache 2.0.

1.q: A security architect is assessing a cloud provider that shares GPUs between tenants. Research in 2025 showed that Rowhammer-style bit flips in GPU memory could wreck a model’s accuracy. What should the architect ask about FIRST?
o: Whether the GPUs are the newest model available from the vendor
Whether error-correcting code (ECC) memory is enabled on the GPUs
Whether the provider encrypts customer data stored on its disks
Whether tenants may choose the region where their GPUs are hosted
1.why: The GPUHammer research flipped bits in GPU memory and collapsed model accuracy. NVIDIA’s guidance was to enable ECC, which detects and corrects such flips at some cost in capacity and speed. Newer hardware, disk encryption and region choice don’t address it.

1.q: Which artefact BEST reveals untested areas in a red team exercise, by mapping what was attempted across the system?
o: The rules of engagement, which set scope, limits and stop rules
A coverage matrix of technique classes against each component
The executive summary, which leads with the business impact
The vulnerability register, which tracks findings to closure
1.why: A coverage matrix maps technique classes against components, showing what has and hasn’t been tested.

1.q: Testers are given an assistant’s system prompts, code, configuration and model weights before starting. Which kind of testing is this?
o: Black box testing, with no internal knowledge of the system
White box testing, with full access to internal details
Grey box testing, with some limited internal knowledge
Bug bounty testing, by external researchers for rewards
1.why: White box testing gives testers full access, including code, configuration and sometimes weights, enabling deeper analysis than black box testing.

1.q: An automated red-teaming pipeline replays the same fixed list of attack prompts every night and no longer finds anything new. Which addition would MOST directly make its attacks adapt to the target?
o: A scorer that labels each of the target’s responses as safe or unsafe
An attacker model that generates and refines attacks using feedback
A larger database for storing the full transcripts of every run
A dashboard charting the attack success rate across releases
1.why: An attacker model generates new attempts and refines them based on the target’s responses and the scorer’s verdicts, as in PAIR-style loops. Scorers, storage and dashboards are needed too, but none of them creates new attacks.

1.q: A company’s small internal red team tests its AI assistant before each release, but researchers keep publishing new jailbreak techniques. Which addition would BEST broaden its coverage?
o: Asking the internal team to repeat its existing tests more often
An AI bug bounty, bringing in many external researchers continuously
Disabling the assistant until every public technique has been fixed
Relying on the model provider’s testing instead of internal testing
1.why: A bug bounty adds many external researchers with diverse techniques, testing continuously between releases. It complements, rather than replaces, internal red teaming.

1.q: A red team is scoping tests for an agent that can approve supplier payments. Which test is MOST specific to the agentic nature of this system?
o: Checking the web interface for cross-site scripting flaws
Checking whether injected content can make it act without approval
Checking the model’s accuracy on a general knowledge benchmark
Checking that the login page enforces a strong password policy
1.why: What makes an agent different is that it acts. Tests must check whether manipulated inputs can drive high-impact actions, such as payments, around approval controls. The other tests apply to ordinary applications too.

1.q: A company runs an email-reading assistant similar to the one hit by 2025’s EchoLeak flaw, in which a crafted email made the assistant leak data with no user action. Which control would MOST reduce the impact of a similar flaw?
o: Training staff never to click on links in suspicious-looking emails
Restricting outbound channels, such as links and images in its output
Making the email server’s spam filter far more sensitive to junk mail
Switching the assistant to the newest model version available
1.why: EchoLeak needed no clicks: injected instructions made the assistant embed data in links and images that were fetched automatically. Restricting what output can reach, and isolating untrusted email content, limits exfiltration. User training doesn’t help against zero-click attacks.

1.q: A red teamer’s successful attack transcript runs to 40 turns, and the developers say they can’t tell what caused the failure. What should the tester do FIRST?
o: Send the full 40-turn transcript again, with more detailed notes
Reduce it to a minimal case that still reproduces the failure
Rate the finding as low severity, since it is hard to reproduce
Close the finding until the developers have time to study it
1.why: A minimal reproducible case isolates the essential trigger, which speeds diagnosis, fixing and regression testing. Long transcripts hide the cause, and difficulty explaining a failure says nothing about its severity.

1.q: Which standard describes how a vendor should handle vulnerability reports internally, from receipt through to remediation?
o: ISO/IEC 29147, the standard for vulnerability disclosure
ISO/IEC 30111, the standard for vulnerability handling
ISO/IEC 42001, the standard for AI management systems
ISO/IEC 27005, the standard for information security risk
1.why: ISO/IEC 30111 covers vendors’ internal vulnerability handling. ISO/IEC 29147 covers disclosure: receiving reports and publishing advisories.

1.q: Two findings have the same impact. One needs an attacker with internal network access and specialist skills; the other works for anyone with a free account. Which prioritisation is BEST?
o: Equal priority, since severity depends only on the impact
Higher priority for the one that needs no special access or skill
Higher priority for the one that needs specialist skills
Lower priority for both, until one of them is actively exploited
1.why: With equal impact, the finding that is easier to exploit, by more people, carries more risk and should be fixed first. Exploitability is a core factor in severity and priority.

1.q: An agent can trigger actions from a fixed list but is never shown what they return, so their outputs can’t influence it. Which design pattern is this?
o: The plan-then-execute pattern, fixing a plan before reading data
The action-selector pattern, strictly one-way by construction
The dual LLM pattern, with privileged and quarantined models
The map-reduce pattern, processing items in isolated workers
1.why: The action-selector pattern lets an agent choose actions without feeding their outputs back to it, so injected tool results can’t influence later steps.

1.q: A risk review finds that a customer-facing assistant can be tricked into revealing other customers’ order details. A full redesign will take three months. What should the team do FIRST?
o: Wait for the redesign, since interim fixes would waste engineering time
Apply interim controls, such as tighter access checks, and track the risk
Accept the risk until the redesign, without recording the decision
Turn off logging, so any leaked details aren’t stored anywhere
1.why: When the full fix takes time, interim compensating controls reduce exposure now, and the residual risk is recorded with an owner and a deadline. Waiting, or accepting the risk informally, leaves customers exposed.

1.q: After turning a user’s request into a structured database query, an agent removes the original request text from its context before writing the answer. Which pattern is this?
o: Context stuffing, filling requests to the maximum input length
Context minimisation, keeping only what later steps need
Context budgeting, reserving space for key instructions
Spotlighting, marking untrusted content inside the prompt
1.why: Context minimisation removes content that later steps don’t need, so any injected text in it can’t influence them.

1.q: Which technology embeds imperceptible watermarks in AI-generated images, audio and text, so they can be detected later?
o: C2PA, which attaches signed provenance metadata to files
SynthID, developed by Google DeepMind for generated media
Safetensors, which stores model weights without executable code
Croissant, which describes datasets with machine-readable metadata
1.why: SynthID embeds watermarks in the content itself, which can survive some edits, while C2PA metadata can be stripped. Neither is proof on its own.

2.q: A spam filter estimates only how likely an email is to be spam, given its contents, without modelling how emails are written. What kind of model is this?
o: A generative model, which learns how the data itself is produced
A discriminative model, which learns the boundary between classes
A reinforcement learner, which improves through rewards for actions
A symbolic system, which applies rules written by human experts
2.why: Discriminative models learn to separate classes, estimating the label from the input. Generative models learn the data distribution itself and can create new samples.

2.q: Before training starts, a data scientist sets the learning rate, batch size and number of epochs. What are these settings called?
o: Parameters, which the model learns from its training data
Hyperparameters, set by people rather than learned in training
Features, which are the input variables that the model uses
Labels, which are the answers the model learns to predict
2.why: Hyperparameters are set to control the learning process. Parameters, such as weights, are learned from the data.

2.q: Which description BEST fits a foundation model?
o: A small model built by hand for one narrow, fixed task
A large model pre-trained on broad data, then adapted to many uses
A rule-based system that encodes the specialist knowledge of human experts
A database of approved answers that a chatbot looks up directly
2.why: Foundation models are pre-trained at scale on broad data, then adapted by prompting or fine-tuning to many downstream tasks, so their flaws can spread widely.

2.q: A company plans to run a small language model directly on employees’ laptops. Which hardware component is designed for this kind of on-device work?
o: A hard disk drive, which stores the model files between sessions
A neural processing unit, which accelerates inference efficiently
A network interface card, which handles traffic to the internet
A trusted platform module, which stores keys for disk encryption
2.why: NPUs accelerate AI workloads with low power use on laptops and phones. On-device AI keeps data local, but moves models and their protection to endpoints.

2.q: A fraud system applies hand-written rules, such as blocking transfers over £10,000 to new payees. Which AI approach is this?
o: Deep learning, which learns layered features from raw data
Symbolic AI, which reasons with explicit, human-authored logic
Unsupervised learning, which finds structure without labels
Generative AI, which creates new content from learned patterns
2.why: Symbolic AI uses explicit rules and logic written by people. It is predictable and auditable but brittle, so it is often combined with learned models.

2.q: A newly appointed AI governance lead needs an organisation-wide structure for handling AI risks, rather than a catalogue of specific attacks. Which resource fits BEST?
o: MITRE ATLAS, a knowledge base of adversary tactics and techniques
The NIST AI Risk Management Framework and its four core functions
The OWASP Top 10 for LLM Applications, a ranked list of key risks
The AI Incident Database, a public collection of reported failures
2.why: The NIST AI RMF is a risk management framework, organised into govern, map, measure and manage. ATLAS catalogues attacker techniques, the OWASP list ranks application risks and the incident database records past failures: useful inputs, but not a management framework.

2.q: A developer sets top-p (nucleus sampling) to 0.1 for an LLM. What effect does this have?
o: The model may only use 10% of its context window in each request
Sampling uses only the smallest token set covering 10% probability
Only 10% of requests are answered, to keep the provider’s costs down
The model’s weights are compressed to 10% of their original size
2.why: Top-p restricts sampling to the smallest set of tokens whose probabilities add up to p. A low value makes output more focused and predictable.

2.q: A RAG assistant uses relevant passages placed at the start and end of a long prompt, but often overlooks those placed in between. What is this effect called?
o: Model collapse, where training on synthetic data erodes quality
Lost in the middle, where models underuse mid-context content
Catastrophic forgetting, where fine-tuning erases earlier skills
Hallucination, where a model invents content with no support
2.why: Models tend to use information at the start and end of long contexts best. Re-ranking and careful placement of key passages help.

2.q: A RAG pipeline fetches 50 candidate passages quickly, then uses a slower, more accurate model to put them in a better order before passing the top five on. What is this second step?
o: Chunking, which splits documents into smaller passages
Re-ranking, which rescores the shortlist more precisely
Embedding, which converts text into numeric vectors
Fine-tuning, which retrains the model on new data
2.why: Re-ranking applies a more accurate model to an initial candidate set, improving which passages reach the prompt.

2.q: A company lets its procurement agent delegate tasks to suppliers’ agents over an agent-to-agent (A2A) protocol. Which control is MOST important for these exchanges?
o: Allowing any agent that supports the protocol to submit tasks freely
Authenticating each remote agent, and treating its results as untrusted
Sharing the procurement agent’s credentials with each supplier’s agent
Turning off logging of agent messages to protect supplier confidentiality
2.why: A2A standardises how agents discover each other and exchange tasks, but trust must still be established: authenticate remote agents, authorise what they may request, and treat what they return as untrusted input that could carry injection.

2.q: An LLM app is given more functionality, permissions and autonomy than its task needs, so a manipulated output can cause real damage. Which OWASP LLM Top 10 risk is this?
o: Sensitive information disclosure, through model outputs
Excessive agency, a design flaw rather than a model bug
Supply chain vulnerabilities, from third-party components
Unbounded consumption, from uncontrolled resource use
2.why: Excessive agency (LLM06) comes from too much functionality, permission or autonomy. Limit tools, scope permissions and require approval for high-impact actions.

2.q: A RAG service’s exact vector search over 200 million embeddings is too slow for interactive use. Which change BEST restores responsiveness while keeping results useful?
o: Cutting the index down to the 1,000 most recent documents only
Approximate nearest-neighbour indexing, trading a little recall for speed
Switching from embeddings to keyword search on document titles alone
Running the same exact search on a single, larger database server
2.why: Approximate nearest-neighbour indexes, such as HNSW, find very close matches far faster at scale, at the cost of occasionally missing the true nearest neighbour. Truncating the corpus or dropping semantic search loses far more.

2.q: A fraud team’s analysts are overwhelmed by alerts, most of which turn out to be legitimate transactions, but missing real fraud is very costly. What is the BEST next step?
o: Raise the decision threshold sharply, accepting whatever fraud is missed
Tune the threshold from the costs of misses and false alarms, then monitor
Lower the threshold, so that even more transactions are flagged
Remove the model and return to reviewing every transaction by hand
2.why: Moving the threshold trades precision against recall. The right point depends on the relative costs of missed fraud and wasted analyst time, so it should be set from those costs and monitored, not pushed to one extreme.

2.q: A team tunes its chatbot until it tops one public benchmark, but users find it worse at their real tasks. Which principle BEST explains this?
o: Moore’s law, which predicts steadily rising computing power over time
Goodhart’s law: a measure that becomes a target stops measuring well
Occam’s razor, which prefers the simplest available explanation
Metcalfe’s law, which links network value to the number of users
2.why: When a benchmark becomes the target, optimisation exploits it and it stops reflecting real performance. Evaluate on your own representative tasks.

2.q: A clinical summarisation assistant is unsure whether a medication dose in the notes is correct. Which behaviour is SAFEST?
o: Choose the most likely dose and present it confidently
Flag the doubt or abstain, prompting a human to check it
Leave the dose out silently, so the summary stays short
Replace it with the standard adult dose for that drug
2.why: Abstaining or flagging uncertainty, rather than guessing, reduces harm in high-stakes uses and routes the question to a person.

2.q: Every December the share of fraudulent transactions doubles, while the patterns within fraudulent and legitimate transactions stay the same. Which response is MOST appropriate?
o: Retrain from scratch each December, using only December data
Recalibrate thresholds or probabilities for the expected class balance
Treat it as concept drift, and redesign the features from the ground up
Ignore it, since changes in class balance can’t affect a model’s outputs
2.why: This is label (prior) drift: the class balance changes, but the relationship between features and outcome doesn’t. Adjusting thresholds or recalibrating for the expected balance handles it; concept drift would need retraining or redesign.

2.q: An ISO/IEC 42001 auditor asks why the organisation hasn’t implemented one of the Annex A controls. What is the BEST evidence to provide?
o: An email from the vendor confirming that the control isn’t needed
The statement of applicability, recording why the control was excluded
A copy of the organisation’s general information security policy
A commitment to implement the control before the next audit cycle
2.why: The statement of applicability lists each Annex A control, whether it applies, and the justification for any exclusion, linked to the risk assessment. It is the record auditors expect for this question.

2.q: A governance team maps each of its AI controls to ISO/IEC 42001, the NIST AI RMF and the EU AI Act, so that evidence for one control can be reused for all three. What is this mapping called?
o: A risk register, which records each risk with its owner and rating
A crosswalk, linking equivalent requirements across frameworks
A RACI matrix, which assigns responsibilities for each task
A heat map, which plots risks by their likelihood and impact
2.why: A crosswalk maps equivalent requirements between frameworks, so one control and its evidence can satisfy several obligations.

2.q: A start-up has built a CV-screening system for EU employers, which counts as high-risk under the AI Act. It wants to start selling next month. What must it complete FIRST?
o: A marketing review of its claims about the system’s accuracy and speed
A conformity assessment showing the system meets the Act’s requirements
A voluntary code of conduct registered with an industry association
A fundamental rights impact assessment completed by each employer
2.why: Before a high-risk system is placed on the EU market, its provider must complete a conformity assessment, draw up an EU declaration of conformity, affix the CE marking and register the system. Fundamental rights impact assessments are separate duties of certain deployers.

2.q: A company in the EU wants to use AI to infer employees’ emotions from webcam video during meetings. What is the status of this under the AI Act?
o: Allowed, provided employees are told that the system is in use
Prohibited in workplaces, except for medical or safety reasons
High risk, needing only a conformity assessment before use
Minimal risk, since the data never leaves the company
2.why: Since February 2025, the AI Act has prohibited emotion recognition in workplaces and education, except for medical or safety reasons.

2.q: What is NIST AI 600-1?
o: A certifiable management system standard for organisational AI governance
A generative AI profile of the NIST AI Risk Management Framework
An EU regulation on general-purpose AI model transparency
A catalogue of attack techniques against machine learning
2.why: NIST AI 600-1 is the Generative AI Profile of the AI RMF, describing risks specific to generative AI and suggested actions.

2.q: A hiring model trained on ten years of past decisions learns to favour candidates who resemble those hired before. Which type of bias is this?
o: Measurement bias, from inaccurate or inconsistent data collection
Historical bias, reproducing inequities that existed in the world
Representation bias, from too few examples of some groups
Automation bias, from people trusting the model too readily
2.why: Historical bias reproduces inequities embedded in past outcomes, even when the data is accurate. Removing it needs deliberate measurement and correction.

2.q: A lender must show that its credit model wrongly approves and wrongly rejects applicants at similar rates for each group. Which fairness criterion BEST matches this requirement?
o: Demographic parity, comparing approval rates across groups
Equalised odds, comparing both kinds of error across groups
Equal opportunity, comparing only the true positive rates
Individual fairness, comparing similar applicants one by one
2.why: Equalised odds requires both the true positive and false positive rates, and so both kinds of error, to be similar across groups. Equal opportunity matches only true positive rates, and demographic parity compares selection rates regardless of outcomes.

2.q: A pricing model explicitly uses customers’ age as an input to give older customers worse offers. Which form of discrimination does this MOST clearly show?
o: Indirect discrimination, through a neutral rule with unequal effects
Direct discrimination, treating people differently by a protected trait
Proxy discrimination, through a feature that stands in for age
Statistical discrimination, from errors in the model’s training data
2.why: Using a protected characteristic directly to treat people less favourably is direct discrimination, or disparate treatment.

2.q: A data centre hosting AI training reports a power usage effectiveness (PUE) of 1.2. What does this mean?
o: The GPUs run at 120% of their rated performance level
Total facility power is 1.2 times the IT equipment’s power
The site uses 1.2 megawatts of power for each server rack
Cooling uses 1.2 times more power than all the IT equipment
2.why: PUE is total facility energy divided by IT equipment energy. A PUE of 1.2 means 20% overhead for cooling, power distribution and other facility needs.

2.q: The board has set a low appetite for AI risks that affect customers. A product team asks how far a chatbot’s error rate may rise above its target before it must escalate. What BEST defines this limit?
o: The product team’s own judgement, made case by case as issues arise
A risk tolerance, defining acceptable variation for that measure
The risk appetite statement alone, without any further detail
The vendor’s published accuracy figures for the underlying model
2.why: Risk appetite is the broad level of risk the organisation accepts; risk tolerance turns it into acceptable variation around specific objectives, such as an error rate, with escalation when it is exceeded.

2.q: Which is the BEST key risk indicator for a customer-facing AI assistant?
o: The number of slides in the assistant’s launch presentation
The weekly rate of successful jailbreak attempts against it
The total number of employees who have heard of the assistant
The date on which the assistant’s contract is next renewed
2.why: A KRI is a measurable signal that risk is rising, such as attack success rates, with thresholds that trigger action.

2.q: A proprietary training dataset is valued at £2 million. A poisoning incident would destroy 30% of its value. What is the single loss expectancy?
o: £6,000,000, the asset value multiplied by thirty
£600,000, the asset value times the exposure factor
£2,000,000, since the whole dataset would be lost
£60,000, the asset value multiplied by three per cent
2.why: SLE = asset value × exposure factor: £2,000,000 × 0.3 = £600,000.

2.q: Which is the BEST-formed AI risk statement?
o: AI is risky, and the company should be very careful when it uses it
Injected emails could make the agent pay fake invoices, losing money
The agent might do something wrong at some point in the future
Prompt injection is listed in the OWASP Top 10 for LLM applications
2.why: A good risk statement links a cause, an event and a consequence, so the risk can be assessed, owned and treated.

2.q: Which assessment focuses on an AI system’s potential consequences for individuals, groups and society, rather than on threats to the organisation’s own assets?
o: A business impact analysis of critical internal processes
An AI system impact assessment, as in ISO/IEC 42005
A penetration test of the system’s external interfaces
A vendor risk review of the system’s supplier
2.why: AI system impact assessments examine effects on people and society, such as rights, fairness and safety, complementing risk assessments focused on the organisation.

2.q: A legal team wants to use a hosted model API for privileged documents. The provider offers “zero data retention”. What should the security team confirm FIRST?
o: That the provider’s model has the highest benchmark scores available
Exactly what is and isn’t retained, including any abuse-monitoring logs
That the provider stores prompts in the same region as the legal team
That staff use the API only during normal working hours
2.why: Zero data retention usually means prompts and outputs aren’t stored after the response, but terms vary: some data may still be logged for abuse monitoring, and eligibility can depend on the feature. Confirm the contractual terms before sending privileged material.

2.q: A company wants to rely on legitimate interests as its GDPR lawful basis for training a model on customer data. What must it do?
o: Nothing more, since legitimate interests covers all business uses
Carry out a balancing test of its interests against people’s rights
Obtain explicit written consent from every customer beforehand
Register the training with the European Commission in advance
2.why: Legitimate interests requires a purpose test, a necessity test and a balancing test against individuals’ rights and expectations, documented in advance.

2.q: A rights holder wants to know whether a general-purpose AI model on the EU market was trained on its catalogue. Which provider obligation under the AI Act MOST directly helps?
o: Publishing the full training dataset for anyone to download
Publishing a sufficiently detailed summary of the training content
Registering every training document in the EU database for AI systems
Notifying each rights holder individually before training begins
2.why: Providers of general-purpose AI models must publish a sufficiently detailed summary of the content used for training, following the Commission’s template, and have a policy to comply with EU copyright law, including opt-outs. They needn’t publish the data itself.

2.q: A consumer fitness app collects users’ heart rate data. It has no relationship with any healthcare provider or health plan. Is this data PHI under HIPAA?
o: Yes, because all health-related data in the US counts as PHI
No: HIPAA covers only covered entities and business associates
Yes, but only once the app has more than 10,000 users
No, because heart rate data is never considered to be health data
2.why: HIPAA applies to covered entities and their business associates. Consumer apps outside that scope aren’t bound by it, though other laws, such as state privacy laws or the FTC Act, may apply.

2.q: An EU insurer plans to outsource claims triage to an AI service provider. Which regulation MOST directly sets requirements for how it manages this ICT third-party risk?
o: The NIS2 Directive, which covers essential and important entities
DORA, the Digital Operational Resilience Act for financial entities
The Data Act, which governs access to data from connected products
The Cyber Resilience Act, covering products with digital elements
2.why: DORA applies to banks, insurers and other financial entities, setting ICT risk management, incident reporting, resilience testing and third-party risk requirements, including contract terms and a register of ICT providers. It takes precedence over NIS2 for these entities.

2.q: A model runs inside a trusted execution environment. Which threat may still apply?
o: Theft of the weights by reading the host’s memory directly
Side-channel attacks that infer data from timing or power use
Tampering with the model by the cloud operator’s administrators
Inspection of decrypted prompts by the hypervisor on the host
2.why: TEEs isolate data from the host and operator, but side channels, such as timing, power or cache behaviour, can still leak information and need mitigation.

2.q: A contract with an AI service provider says it will “take security seriously” and “respond promptly” to incidents. What is the BEST improvement before signing?
o: Add a clause saying that the provider will follow industry best practice
Define measurable commitments, such as patching and notification times
Remove the security terms and rely on the provider’s good reputation
Ask the provider for a brochure describing its security team
2.why: Vague promises can’t be enforced or monitored. A security SLA with defined metrics, such as patching windows, incident notification deadlines and audit rights, makes commitments measurable.

2.q: A company rents cloud GPU virtual machines and installs its own operating system and inference server to host a model. Who is responsible for patching the inference server?
o: The cloud provider, since it owns the physical GPU hardware
The company, since it manages everything above the hypervisor
The model’s original developer, since it wrote the weights
No one, since inference servers don’t need patching at all
2.why: In infrastructure as a service, the provider secures the physical and virtualisation layers; the customer secures the OS, software, data and access it installs.

2.q: Which tool can discover employees’ use of cloud AI applications and enforce policies, such as blocking uploads of sensitive files to unapproved services?
o: A vulnerability scanner that checks servers for missing patches
A cloud access security broker, between users and SaaS services
A web application firewall that protects the company’s own websites
A hardware security module that stores and protects encryption keys
2.why: CASBs discover sanctioned and unsanctioned cloud app use and apply policies, such as DLP controls, between users and cloud services.

2.q: An organisation invites staff to declare any unapproved AI tools they use, without penalty, for one month. What is the MAIN purpose?
o: To identify and then punish the staff who broke the AI policy
To surface shadow AI so it can be assessed and safely enabled
To reduce the number of AI licences the company pays for
To collect evidence for any disciplinary hearings later on
2.why: An amnesty encourages honest disclosure of shadow AI, so the organisation can assess the tools and offer approved alternatives rather than drive use underground.

2.q: Auditors ask how a training dataset was collected, what it contains and which uses it is unsuitable for, but the team has only a model card. Which document would BEST answer them?
o: A second model card, describing the model’s performance in more depth
A datasheet for datasets, documenting its collection and composition
A system prompt explaining the dataset’s purpose to the model itself
A press release announcing the dataset and its origins to the public
2.why: Datasheets for datasets document why a dataset was created, its composition, how it was collected and processed, and recommended and unsuitable uses. Model cards describe models, not their data.

2.q: An organisation wants AI security training that matches what each role actually needs, from executives to ML engineers. What should it develop FIRST?
o: A single course that every employee completes once each year
A competency framework, defining skills and proficiency levels
A phishing simulation based on realistic AI-generated emails
A list of approved AI tools posted on the company intranet
2.why: A competency framework sets out the skills each role needs at defined proficiency levels, so training can be targeted and progress measured. One-size-fits-all courses miss role-specific needs.

2.q: A CISO wants an early warning that AI security culture is weakening, before incidents occur. Which metric is the BEST leading indicator?
o: The number of confirmed AI-related data leaks in the last quarter
How often staff report near misses, such as unsafe prompts they spotted
The total cost of AI incidents recorded in the annual report
The number of regulatory fines received for AI-related breaches
2.why: Leading indicators, such as near-miss reporting and engagement with training, change before harm occurs. Leaks, incident costs and fines are lagging indicators: they confirm problems after the event.

2.q: A training dataset has inconsistent field definitions and missing metadata, and its owner has no time to deal with it. Which role is MOST appropriate to take day-to-day charge of fixing this?
o: The data custodian, who runs the storage platform and its backups
The data steward, who looks after the data’s quality and documentation
The data subject, whose personal data happens to appear in the dataset
The external auditor, who reviews the dataset and its controls yearly
2.why: Data stewards look after data quality, definitions, metadata and standards day to day, while the owner remains accountable. Custodians operate the technical environment.

2.q: An auditor asks where a dataset originally came from, how it was collected and what rights apply to it. Which record answers this?
o: Data lineage, tracing how data flowed into datasets and models
Data provenance, documenting the data’s background and terms
Chain of custody, logging who held or transferred the data
Dataset versioning, recording each change as a new version
2.why: Provenance records origin, collection method, rights and history. Lineage records how data flows and is transformed; chain of custody records who held it.

2.q: An AI vendor builds a search index from a client’s documents, strictly on the client’s instructions and for that client only. What is the vendor’s GDPR role?
o: Controller, because it hosts the documents on its own servers
Processor, since the client decides the purposes and means
Joint controller, because it chooses which model to use
Data subject, because its staff can read the documents
2.why: A processor handles personal data on a controller’s behalf. The client decides the purposes and means; a vendor that used the data for its own purposes would become a controller.

2.q: Two banks agree to pool customer transaction data and co-develop a shared fraud model for both of them. What is their GDPR relationship?
o: Controller and processor, with the larger bank as controller
Joint controllers, needing an arrangement setting out duties
Independent processors, each acting for the model vendor
No relationship, since fraud prevention is exempt from the GDPR
2.why: Parties that jointly determine the purposes and means of processing are joint controllers. They need an arrangement setting out their respective responsibilities.

2.q: A new training batch contains customer ages of −3 and 240, and a date field in the wrong format. Which control should catch this before training?
o: Encryption of the batch at rest with a customer-managed key
Schema and range validation when the data is ingested
A larger model that can learn to ignore unusual values
Manual review of the model’s outputs after deployment
2.why: Validation at ingestion checks schemas, types and value ranges, quarantining bad batches before they can corrupt training.

2.q: A released dataset is 5-anonymous, but in one group of five records everyone has the same diagnosis. What weakness does this show?
o: Too few records overall, since k-anonymity needs at least 100
A lack of l-diversity, so the sensitive value is still revealed
Excessive generalisation, which makes the data useless for research
A breach of HIPAA, since diagnoses can never be released at all
2.why: k-anonymity hides who is who within a group, but if everyone in the group shares a sensitive value, it leaks anyway. l-diversity requires varied sensitive values.

2.q: A US hospital wants to share patient notes with an AI developer as de-identified data under HIPAA, but the notes contain dates of service and five-digit ZIP codes. Which approach BEST meets the Safe Harbor method?
o: Remove the names only, since dates and ZIP codes aren’t identifiers
Remove all 18 listed identifiers, including most date and ZIP detail
Encrypt the notes, since encrypted data always counts as de-identified
Ask each patient to confirm they are happy for their notes to be shared
2.why: Safe Harbor requires removing 18 types of identifiers, including all elements of dates except the year and most geographic detail (only the first three ZIP digits may stay, and only for areas of more than 20,000 people), with no actual knowledge that what remains could identify anyone. The alternative is expert determination.

2.q: A health research team must publish a model trained on patient records, and wants a provable limit on what the model reveals about any one patient. Which training approach BEST meets this goal?
o: Training on pseudonymised records, with names replaced by tokens
DP-SGD, with per-example clipping, noise and a privacy accountant
Training for fewer epochs, so the model memorises less of the data
Encrypting the model’s weights before the model is published
2.why: Only differentially private training gives a provable bound on what can be learned about any one record. Pseudonymisation, early stopping and encryption reduce some risks but give no such guarantee.

2.q: A hospital’s AI scribe vendor asks for full patient records to improve its model, though the service only needs the current visit’s notes. Which HIPAA principle limits this?
o: The breach notification rule, which governs reporting incidents
The minimum necessary standard for uses and disclosures of PHI
The right of access, which lets patients obtain their records
The security rule’s encryption requirement for stored PHI
2.why: The minimum necessary standard limits uses and disclosures of PHI to the minimum needed for the purpose, so full records shouldn’t be shared for this.

2.q: A team plans to send full customer profiles to a model that only uses each customer’s purchase categories. Which GDPR principle does this breach?
o: Accuracy, since the profiles may contain outdated details
Data minimisation, since extra fields add risk without benefit
Integrity, since the profiles could be changed in transit
Transparency, since customers weren’t told about the new model
2.why: Data minimisation limits personal data to what is adequate, relevant and necessary for the purpose. Send only the fields the model uses.

2.q: Before a fraud model is retrained, an insider marks a subset of fraudulent transactions as “legitimate” in the training data. What attack is this?
o: Model inversion, reconstructing training data from outputs
Label flipping, a form of targeted training data poisoning
Membership inference, revealing which records were used
Evasion, altering inputs at inference to avoid detection
2.why: Label flipping alters training labels so the model learns wrong associations, here letting certain fraud pass. Separation of duties and label audits help.

2.q: An attacker’s goal is to degrade a model’s accuracy across all inputs, rather than to cause specific errors. Which type of poisoning is this?
o: Targeted poisoning, aimed at particular inputs or classes
Availability poisoning, which damages overall performance
Backdoor poisoning, triggered by a hidden input pattern
Clean-label poisoning, which keeps every label correct
2.why: Availability poisoning degrades overall performance. Targeted and backdoor poisoning cause specific misbehaviour while keeping normal accuracy.

2.q: A training job pulls thousands of files from a shared bucket. The team needs assurance that every approved file is present and unaltered, and that nothing extra was added. Which control BEST provides this?
o: Checking that the bucket’s total size matches last week’s figure
A signed manifest of hashes, verified against the contents before use
Restricting the bucket, so that only the training job can read from it
Scanning the files with antivirus software before every training run
2.why: A signed manifest lists every approved file with its hash. Verifying it before training detects missing, altered or extra files, and the signature proves the manifest itself wasn’t tampered with. Size checks, access restrictions and antivirus don’t prove integrity.

2.q: Just before a scheduled training run, one dataset file’s hash doesn’t match the approved manifest. What should happen?
o: Train anyway, since one file is a tiny share of the dataset
Stop the run, quarantine the file and investigate the change
Recalculate the hash and update the manifest to match the file
Delete the file and train on the remaining data straight away
2.why: A mismatch means the data may have been tampered with. Stop, quarantine and investigate, then restore the approved version before training.

2.q: A team suspects that a few thousand poisoned samples are hidden among 20 million training examples, but doesn’t know which. Which technique is the BEST place to start looking?
o: Manually reading a random sample of 500 training examples
Searching for unusual clusters and outliers in embedding space
Retraining the model with a different random seed and comparing
Deleting the oldest 10% of the training data, to be on the safe side
2.why: Poisoned samples often form tight, unusual clusters or outliers in embedding or activation space, which can be found at scale. A small random sample will probably miss them, and arbitrary deletion doesn’t target the poison.

2.q: A model-serving service calls a feature store over the internal network. Which control authenticates both sides of each connection?
o: Standard TLS, where only the server presents a certificate
Mutual TLS, with certificates on the client and the server
IP allow-listing, which permits traffic from known addresses
API keys sent in plain text within each request header
2.why: Mutual TLS authenticates client and server with certificates and encrypts traffic, supporting Zero Trust between internal services.

2.q: A company is setting up model signing for its releases. Which approach to protecting the root signing key is BEST?
o: Storing it in an encrypted file on the build server’s local disk
Generating and keeping it in a hardware security module, offline
Keeping it in the source code repository, where changes are tracked
Emailing it to the release managers, so that any of them can sign
2.why: A root key generated and held in an HSM never leaves in plain form, and keeping the root offline, with day-to-day signing done by subordinate keys, limits exposure. Files, repositories and email all risk theft.

2.q: Old SSDs that held confidential training data will be reused by another department. Which sanitisation approach is MOST appropriate under NIST SP 800-88?
o: Deleting the files, then quick-formatting each of the drives
Purge, for example by cryptographic erase or block erase
Destroy, by shredding the drives before they are reused
None, since the application had already encrypted the data
2.why: Purge makes recovery infeasible even with laboratory techniques while leaving the media usable. For SSDs, cryptographic or block erase is preferred because wear levelling defeats simple overwriting. Destroy prevents reuse, and deleting or formatting leaves data recoverable.

2.q: A DSPM scan finds forgotten copies of training data in old cloud buckets, outside any governed store. What are these copies called?
o: Synthetic data, generated to stand in for the real records
Shadow data, which often escapes security controls entirely
Golden data, kept as the trusted reference version
Derived data, such as embeddings created from documents
2.why: Shadow data is unmanaged or forgotten copies outside governed stores. It often lacks controls and owners, so DSPM tools hunt for it.

2.q: A team runs the current model version in one production environment and the new version in an identical second one, switching traffic between them. What is this approach?
o: A canary release, sending a small share of traffic to the new version
A blue/green deployment, where rollback is almost instantaneous
A shadow deployment, where users never see the new outputs
A big-bang release, replacing the old version everywhere at once
2.why: Blue/green deployments keep two production environments and switch traffic between them, so rollback is immediate.

2.q: A model is about to be approved for production. The approval board asks how anyone will know if it starts to degrade. Which approval condition BEST answers this?
o: A promise from the developers to keep a close eye on the model
A monitoring plan with metrics, thresholds, frequency and an owner
A one-off accuracy test, to be repeated only if users complain
A rule that the model is retrained every week, whatever happens
2.why: Approval should include a monitoring plan that defines the metrics, thresholds, review frequency and owner, so degradation triggers action. Informal watching and complaint-driven testing find problems too late.

2.q: Which discipline, long required of banks, governs models through sound development, independent validation and ongoing oversight?
o: Agile delivery, which favours working software over documents
Model risk management, as set out in the US SR 11-7 guidance
ITIL service management, which handles incidents and changes
Six Sigma, which reduces defects in manufacturing processes
2.why: Model risk management, set out for US banks in SR 11-7, requires sound development, effective challenge through independent validation, and governance.

2.q: Every AI model, from a low-risk internal spell-checker to a credit decision engine, goes through the same lengthy approval process. Teams complain, and some bypass it. What is the BEST fix?
o: Abolish approvals for internal models, keeping them for external ones
Tier the workflow, scaling evidence and approvers to each model’s risk
Add more approvers, so that the same process can run more quickly
Discipline the teams that bypassed it, and keep the process unchanged
2.why: A risk-tiered workflow sets the evidence, approvers, conditions and review cycle for each tier, so low-risk models move quickly and high-risk ones get rigorous scrutiny. One heavy process for everything encourages bypassing.

2.q: When its main model is overloaded, a chatbot switches to shorter answers and turns off image analysis, rather than failing completely. What is this?
o: Fail open, which serves unchecked responses when controls fail
Graceful degradation, scaling the service back step by step
Load testing, which measures performance under expected traffic
Model drift, where performance slowly changes over time
2.why: Graceful degradation keeps a reduced but safe service running during failure or overload, rather than failing outright.

2.q: A public chatbot’s monthly bill has spiked. A few accounts are sending extremely long prompts that request maximum-length outputs, around the clock. Which response BEST addresses the root cause?
o: Upgrading to a larger plan, so the service can absorb the load
Per-user limits on input, output tokens, rate and spend, with alerts
Blocking the accounts involved, then taking no further action
Adding a notice asking users to keep their prompts short
2.why: This is unbounded consumption (OWASP LLM10). The root cause is missing limits: per-user caps on input size, output tokens, request rate and spend, with monitoring and alerts. Blocking a few accounts treats the symptom.

2.q: A model API must stop any one customer exceeding its paid monthly allowance, and also stop short spikes that slow the service for others. Which combination is BEST?
o: A monthly quota alone, since it already limits total consumption
A quota for monthly totals, plus a rate limit per short interval
A rate limit alone, since it controls both spikes and totals
Neither, relying on customers to manage their own usage fairly
2.why: A quota caps total use over a period, such as a month; a rate limit caps use per short interval, protecting shared capacity from spikes. Each controls something the other doesn’t.

2.q: A team verifies downloaded model files against MD5 checksums published on the same website. What is the BEST improvement?
o: Checking the MD5 values twice, on two different machines
Verifying signatures over SHA-256 digests from a trusted source
Downloading the files over HTTPS, then skipping the checksums
Renaming the files after download, so attackers can’t find them
2.why: MD5 is broken, so a crafted file could match, and checksums published alongside the file can be replaced by whoever controls the site. Signatures over strong digests such as SHA-256, verified with keys from a trusted source, prove both integrity and origin.

2.q: Research showed that a model trained to behave harmfully only when a trigger appears kept this behaviour even after standard safety training. What is such a model called?
o: A rogue agent, acting outside its intended purpose
A sleeper agent, a notably hard case for safety testing
A distilled model, trained to imitate a larger model
A foundation model, pre-trained on broad web data
2.why: Sleeper agents behave normally until triggered, and research found the behaviour can survive safety training, so provenance matters as much as testing.

2.q: A jailbreak that works on a popular open-weight base model also works on many fine-tunes built from it. What is this called?
o: Concentration risk, from many services relying on a single provider
An inherited vulnerability, passed down through the model family
Safety erosion, where fine-tuning weakens refusals over time
Typosquatting, where look-alike names mislead developers
2.why: Weaknesses in a base model, such as a working jailbreak, carry over to models built on it, so advisories about a base model apply to its derivatives.

2.q: An engineer downloads a model from a community mirror, and its SHA-256 hash matches the value shown on the same mirror. Before deployment, what is the MOST important additional check?
o: Recalculating the hash on a second machine to confirm the match
Verifying the publisher’s signature, or the official source’s hash
Checking that the file size is close to the size the mirror lists
Scanning the download folder with the endpoint antivirus tool
2.why: A hash shown next to the file only proves the file matches what the mirror claims, and whoever controls the mirror controls both. Authenticity needs a signature, or a hash obtained from the original publisher through a trusted channel.

2.q: A supply chain review for an AI product covered only code dependencies and container images. Which gap is MOST important to close?
o: Extending the review to the build server’s operating system patches
Adding pre-trained models, datasets, adapters and model hosting services
Reviewing the marketing materials published about the product
Repeating the same review with a second scanning tool for comparison
2.why: AI systems depend on components that traditional reviews miss: pre-trained models, datasets, fine-tuning adapters, embedding models and hosted model services. Each can carry poisoning, backdoors or licensing problems.

2.q: An AI vendor signs a “Secure by Design” pledge. What does this commitment mainly mean for its customers?
o: Customers must add all security controls themselves after purchase
The vendor builds security in, rather than leaving it to customers
The vendor’s products are guaranteed never to have vulnerabilities
Customers receive the product’s source code for their own review
2.why: Secure by Design shifts responsibility to vendors to build in protections, such as secure defaults and MFA, rather than leaving customers to add them.

2.q: A malicious MCP server’s tool description quietly changes how an agent uses a different, trusted server’s tools. What is this attack?
o: A rug pull, where a tool’s own behaviour changes after approval
Tool shadowing, a cross-server variant of tool poisoning attacks
Token passthrough, forwarding a client’s token to other APIs
Typosquatting, registering a server with a look-alike name
2.why: In tool shadowing, one server’s tool description manipulates how the agent uses other servers’ tools. Vet servers and isolate trust between them.

2.q: In the Model Context Protocol, which component does the AI application create to talk to each individual server?
o: The MCP host, which is the AI application as a whole
The MCP client, which manages that single connection
The MCP server, which exposes tools and resources
The model provider, which hosts the language model
2.why: The host is the AI application; it creates an MCP client for each server connection. Servers expose tools, resources and prompts.

2.q: A team compares self-hosting an open-weight model with using a hosted API. Why must total cost of ownership include more than GPU prices?
o: GPU prices always fall, so they can be left out of the estimate
Self-hosting adds staff, patching, monitoring and security work
Hosted APIs are always free for the first year of any contract
Open-weight licences always require large annual payments
2.why: TCO for self-hosting includes skilled staff, patching, monitoring, security, capacity and resilience, not just hardware.

2.q: A STRIDE review of a model registry finds that anyone with storage access could replace model weights. Which control category MOST directly addresses this threat?
o: Logging every read of the model files, for review after any incident
Integrity controls, such as signing models and restricting all writes
Rate limiting the API that serves predictions from the model to users
Encrypting network traffic between users and the model’s API endpoint
2.why: Replacing weights is tampering, so the answer is integrity: signing with verification, immutable or tightly controlled storage, and change logging. Read logs, rate limits and transport encryption address other STRIDE categories.

2.q: A training data bucket was accidentally made public by a change to an infrastructure-as-code file, and nobody noticed for weeks. Which control would BEST stop this happening again?
o: A quarterly manual review of the permissions on all cloud storage
Automated policy checks on IaC changes, before they are released
A data loss prevention policy applied to the bucket’s contents
Encrypting the bucket’s contents with a customer-managed key
2.why: Scanning infrastructure-as-code in the pipeline catches misconfigurations, such as public buckets, before they reach production, and can block the change. Manual quarterly reviews are slow, and DLP or encryption don’t stop a bucket being public.

2.q: Which resource provides consensus hardening settings for the operating systems and Kubernetes clusters that host AI models?
o: The OWASP Top 10, which lists common web application risks
The CIS Benchmarks, published for many platforms and services
MITRE ATLAS, which catalogues adversary techniques against AI
ISO/IEC 42001, which specifies an AI management system
2.why: CIS Benchmarks give consensus-based secure configuration guidance for operating systems, containers, Kubernetes and cloud services.

2.q: A platform team must run inference for two business units with very different data sensitivity on the same GPUs. Which sharing approach provides the BEST isolation?
o: Time-slicing, in which the two workloads take turns on the whole GPU
Hardware partitioning, giving each unit its own memory and compute
Running both units’ models in the same container for efficiency
Allocating GPU time to whichever unit asks first, on demand
2.why: Hardware partitioning, such as NVIDIA Multi-Instance GPU, gives each instance dedicated memory and compute slices, so tenants are isolated in hardware. Time-slicing shares memory and compute in turn, a much weaker boundary; dedicated GPUs are stronger still.

2.q: A company is designing fire suppression for a data hall full of GPU servers, and wants to minimise the risk of water damage from a burst pipe or an accidental activation. Which system fits BEST?
o: A wet-pipe sprinkler system, with water held in the pipes at all times
A pre-action system, whose pipes fill only after a fire is detected
Portable fire extinguishers alone, placed at the end of every row
A deluge system that floods the whole hall when any alarm sounds
2.why: Pre-action systems keep pipes dry until a detection event, often requiring a second trigger before water flows, which reduces accidental discharge. Clean-agent gaseous systems are another common option. Wet-pipe and deluge systems carry more water risk.

2.q: A Kubernetes cluster serving models must never run an image that hasn’t passed the signing step of the build pipeline. Which control BEST enforces this at deployment time?
o: A wiki page reminding engineers to deploy only signed images
An admission controller that rejects pods with unverified images
A weekly report listing which running images were signed
A network policy blocking traffic between pods in the cluster
2.why: An admission controller, such as a signature-verification policy, checks each pod before it starts and refuses images without valid signatures. Reminders and reports don’t prevent anything, and network policies don’t govern images.

2.q: In a medallion data architecture for AI pipelines, what typically happens as data moves from the bronze layer to the silver layer?
o: The data is deleted, since bronze data is no longer needed
Raw data is validated, cleaned and conformed to standards
The data is published directly to end users without checks
The data is encrypted for the first time before storage
2.why: Medallion architectures move data from raw (bronze) to validated and cleaned (silver) to curated, use-ready (gold) layers.

2.q: A team merges the weights of two fine-tuned models to combine their skills. What should happen before the merged model is used?
o: Nothing, since both parent models were already approved
Verify both parents’ provenance and re-evaluate it as new
Publish it on a public hub, so that others can test it
Rename it, so that it isn’t confused with its parent models
2.why: A merged model is a new artefact that can inherit weaknesses from both parents. Verify their provenance and licences, and evaluate it before approval.

2.q: After approximate unlearning removed certain facts, they reappear when the model is later fine-tuned on unrelated data. What is this effect?
o: Model collapse, from training on the model’s own outputs
Knowledge resurfacing, a sign the information was only hidden
Catastrophic forgetting, where new training erases old skills
Concept drift, where the meaning of labels changes over time
2.why: Knowledge resurfacing shows approximate unlearning may hide rather than remove information. Verify unlearning, or use exact methods where assurance is needed.

2.q: Which technique transforms untrusted text before it enters a prompt, for example by encoding it, so the model can recognise it as data rather than instructions?
o: Few-shot prompting, which adds worked examples to the prompt
Spotlighting, a prompt-level defence that helps but isn’t complete
Context budgeting, which reserves space for key instructions
Chain-of-thought, which asks the model to show its reasoning steps
2.why: Spotlighting delimits, datamarks or encodes untrusted content so the model can tell it apart from instructions. It reduces, but doesn’t eliminate, injection.

2.q: Before a product launch, a team needs to know the maximum load its AI service can handle before it fails, to plan capacity and fallbacks. Which test is BEST?
o: A smoke test that sends a few requests after each deployment
A breakpoint test, adding traffic in steps until it breaks
A soak test at normal load, left running for several days
A unit test of each function in the service’s codebase
2.why: A breakpoint (stress) test raises load in steps until the service fails, revealing its maximum capacity and how it fails. Soak tests find leaks over time at steady load, and smoke and unit tests check basic correctness.

2.q: A team schedules a session in which it simulates its model provider failing, to practise the response and test runbooks. What is this called?
o: A code review, checking changes before they are merged
A game day, a planned exercise based on a realistic failure
A sprint review, showing completed work to stakeholders
A design review, assessing an architecture before it is built
2.why: Game days rehearse realistic failures in a planned way, testing people, runbooks and systems together.

2.q: What does a content policy provide for an AI system’s guardrails?
o: The legal terms that all users must accept before using the service
The rules defining what content is allowed, restricted or blocked
The list of model providers that the organisation has approved
The pricing for each tier of the AI service’s subscriptions
2.why: A content policy defines what is allowed, restricted or blocked, so filters, classifiers and reviewers can enforce it consistently.

2.q: A nightly backend job calls a model API to summarise reports. No user is involved. Which authentication approach is BEST?
o: A named employee’s username and password, stored inside the job
The OAuth 2.0 client credentials grant, with short-lived tokens
The authorisation code flow, prompting someone to sign in each night
A shared API key that every team’s scripts use for convenience
2.why: The client credentials grant lets a service authenticate as itself and obtain short-lived tokens, with no user involved. Personal credentials and shared keys break accountability, and interactive flows need a user.

2.q: Model servers and feature stores across several clusters authenticate to each other with long-lived shared secrets that are rarely rotated. Which approach BEST replaces them?
o: Longer shared secrets, rotated once a year on a fixed, published schedule
Short-lived workload identities issued automatically, as with SPIFFE
IP address allowlists, so that only known servers can connect
Embedding each secret in the container images at build time
2.why: Workload identity systems such as SPIFFE and SPIRE issue short-lived, automatically rotated identities, used for mutual TLS between services. Long-lived shared secrets, IP allowlists and secrets baked into images are all weaker.

2.q: Which protocol, built on OAuth 2.0, lets an AI platform sign users in using ID tokens from the corporate identity provider?
o: SAML 2.0, which exchanges XML assertions between parties
OpenID Connect, widely used for modern single sign-on
SCIM, which provisions and removes user accounts
Kerberos, which issues tickets within a Windows domain
2.why: OpenID Connect adds identity to OAuth 2.0 using ID tokens. SAML uses XML assertions; SCIM provisions accounts.

2.q: An agent signs each request it sends to a payments API, and the API keeps tamper-evident logs. Which property does this MOST directly support?
o: Availability, keeping the payments API online at all times of day
Non-repudiation, so its actions can’t later be credibly denied
Confidentiality, keeping the payment details secret
Elasticity, scaling the API up or down to meet demand
2.why: Signed requests and tamper-evident logs give proof of who did what, supporting non-repudiation for investigations and disputes.

2.q: An organisation’s agents each contain their own hard-coded permission checks, which are inconsistent and hard to audit. Which architectural change BEST fixes this?
o: Asking each team to document its agent’s checks more thoroughly
A central policy decision point, with enforcement in front of each tool
Removing the checks, and relying on the model’s own judgement instead
Giving every agent administrator rights, to simplify the design
2.why: Externalising authorisation to a policy decision point, with enforcement points in front of tools and data, makes decisions consistent, centrally managed and auditable. Documentation alone doesn’t fix inconsistency.

2.q: A policy engine permits an agent’s refund, but only if the refund is logged and the customer is notified. What are these attached conditions called?
o: Exceptions, which waive a policy requirement temporarily
Authorisation obligations, enforced alongside access
Entitlements, which list every permission a role holds
Attestations, which prove how an artefact was built
2.why: Obligations are actions a policy requires alongside a permit decision, such as logging, notification or step-up approval.

2.q: A payments agent should be allowed to pay up to £50 to one specific supplier, rather than make any payment at all. Which OAuth approach BEST expresses this?
o: A broad “payments” scope that covers every type of payment
Rich authorisation requests, with structured details such as amount
A long-lived refresh token granted when the agent is installed
Basic authentication using the account holder’s own password
2.why: Rich authorisation requests (RFC 9396) let a client ask for fine-grained permissions using structured details, such as amount, currency and payee, instead of broad scopes.

2.q: A new tool is added to an agent gateway, but no policy mentions it yet. Under a sound design, what happens when an agent calls it?
o: The call is allowed, since nothing forbids it explicitly
The call is refused until an explicit allow rule exists
The call is allowed only during normal business hours
The call is forwarded to the model to decide for itself
2.why: Deny by default means anything not explicitly allowed is refused, so new tools gain no access until a policy grants it.

2.q: A user grants an assistant full access to their mailbox “to save time”, though it only needs to read one shared folder. What is this?
o: Excessive functionality, as the tool offers too many operations
Over-delegation, handing the assistant much wider authority
Separation of duties, as tasks are split between people
Continuous authorisation, as access is re-evaluated during use
2.why: Over-delegation gives an agent more of the user’s authority than its task requires. Grant narrow, task-scoped access instead.

2.q: When an employee leaves, their account is disabled, but their sessions in the AI platform stay valid for hours until tokens expire. Which capability BEST closes this gap?
o: Longer token lifetimes, so that sessions are checked less often
Continuous access evaluation, with revocation signals such as CAEP
A monthly access review covering all AI platform accounts
Asking managers to tell the AI platform team about leavers
2.why: Continuous access evaluation lets the identity provider signal events such as account disablement to relying applications in near real time, so sessions end at once. Waiting for tokens to expire, or for monthly reviews, leaves a window.

2.q: What is the difference between showback and chargeback for AI usage costs?
o: Showback applies to agents; chargeback applies only to people
Showback reports costs to teams; chargeback actually bills them
They are the same practice, named differently by finance teams
Showback covers training costs; chargeback covers only inference
2.why: Showback makes teams aware of their AI costs; chargeback allocates the costs to their budgets. Both rely on accurate per-identity token accounting.

2.q: An AI admin console logs users out after 15 minutes of inactivity, but a session kept busy by a script can stay open indefinitely. Which control BEST addresses this?
o: Shortening the idle time-out from 15 minutes to just five minutes
An absolute lifetime, forcing a fresh sign-in at a fixed interval
Removing the idle time-out, so that busy users aren’t confused by it
Showing a banner that reminds users to log out when finished
2.why: An absolute lifetime ends every session after a fixed period regardless of activity, forcing re-authentication. A shorter idle time-out doesn’t help with a session that is never idle.

2.q: During a major AI incident, the security, ML and legal teams each make decisions independently, and nobody keeps a single timeline. Which role should be assigned FIRST?
o: A communications officer, to brief the press immediately
An incident lead, who coordinates everyone and owns the decision log
A forensic analyst, to image every affected system straight away
A vendor liaison, to contact the model provider about the issue
2.why: An incident lead coordinates the response across teams, owns the timeline and decision log, and makes sure decisions are made deliberately. Other roles report into that coordination.

2.q: A team runs a fixed set of test prompts against its hosted model every hour, to spot unannounced changes in behaviour. What is this?
o: A load test, measuring response times under heavy traffic
A behavioural canary, an early warning of silent updates
A penetration test, attacking the model to find weaknesses
A tabletop exercise, discussing a simulated incident
2.why: Behavioural canaries run fixed prompts on a schedule, so unannounced model updates or drift show up quickly.

2.q: A company has written new AI incident playbooks but never tested them. It wants to find gaps in roles and decisions cheaply, without touching live systems. Which exercise is BEST to start with?
o: A full-scale live exercise that takes production systems offline
A tabletop exercise, walking the team through a realistic scenario
An unannounced red team attack on the production AI service
An annual review of the playbooks by an external consultancy
2.why: Tabletop exercises talk participants through a scenario to test roles, decisions and communication, exposing gaps cheaply and safely. Functional and full-scale exercises come later, once plans are sound.

2.q: Which combination BEST reflects defence in depth for a production AI assistant?
o: One strong guardrail, relied on to stop every attack
Prevention, detection and tested recovery, in layers
A larger model, assumed to resist manipulation on its own
An annual audit, with no controls in between audits
2.why: Defence in depth layers prevention, detection and recovery, so one failed control doesn’t lead to harm.

2.q: Which open standard is widely used to instrument AI applications for traces, metrics and logs, including conventions for generative AI?
o: STIX, a format for sharing threat intelligence
OpenTelemetry, an open observability framework
SAML, a protocol for single sign-on assertions
CycloneDX, a format for bills of materials
2.why: OpenTelemetry provides vendor-neutral traces, metrics and logs, with semantic conventions for generative AI calls.

2.q: A SOC wants to detect when an agent’s API key starts behaving unusually, such as calling tools it never used before at odd hours, without writing a rule for every case. Which capability fits BEST?
o: Static allowlists of the IP addresses each key may connect from
User and entity behaviour analytics, baselining each key’s activity
A daily export of API logs for analysts to read through manually
Longer retention of API logs, keeping them for seven years
2.why: User and entity behaviour analytics build baselines of normal behaviour for users, agents and keys, and alert on deviations, catching unusual patterns that no specific rule anticipated.

2.q: As each AI alert arrives, a SOC automatically adds the user’s department, the model version and the data classification involved. What is this?
o: Normalisation, mapping fields to a common schema
Event enrichment, adding context for triage
Deduplication, removing repeated alerts
Correlation, linking related events together
2.why: Enrichment adds context, such as identity, asset, model version and data sensitivity, so analysts can triage faster and more accurately.

2.q: Which component scores AI inputs and outputs for safety and quality as they happen in production?
o: An offline benchmark, run once before each release
An online evaluator, such as a classifier or model judge
A model card, which documents intended use and limits
A risk register, which records risks and their owners
2.why: Online evaluators score live traffic as it happens, feeding monitoring, alerts and automatic guards.

2.q: A SOC’s AI detection rules were written ad hoc, nobody knows which still work, and changes sometimes break them silently. Which practice BEST fixes this?
o: Disabling all custom rules and relying on the vendor’s defaults
Detection engineering: rules as code, tested, versioned and tuned
Asking analysts to note in a spreadsheet which rules seem useful
Adding more rules, so that coverage outweighs any broken ones
2.why: Detection engineering treats detections as code: designed against threats, tested with sample data, version-controlled, deployed through a pipeline and tuned over time, so regressions are caught.

2.q: Which threat hunting framework organises each hunt into prepare, execute and act phases, so that every hunt leaves lasting improvements?
o: STRIDE, which classifies threats into six categories
PEAK, introduced by Splunk’s SURGe team in 2023
PASTA, which links threats to business impact
DREAD, which scores threats on five factors
2.why: PEAK (Prepare, Execute, Act with Knowledge) structures hunts, including hypothesis-driven, baseline and model-assisted types, and feeds results into detections.

2.q: A jailbreak detector scores each prompt on its own. Red teamers bypass it by spreading an attack across many harmless-looking turns. Which change BEST improves detection?
o: Raising the detector’s threshold, so that it flags fewer prompts
Analysing whole conversations, as well as each individual prompt
Limiting every conversation to a single prompt and response
Blocking any prompt that contains the word “jailbreak”
2.why: Multi-turn attacks only become visible across turns, so detectors need conversation-level context alongside per-prompt checks. Single-turn limits would break legitimate use, and keyword blocks are trivially avoided.

2.q: Signature-based rules catch known injection phrases, but attackers keep rewording them. Which addition would BEST help catch new, previously unseen attempts?
o: Adding each new phrase to the blocklist as soon as it is reported
Embedding-based anomaly detection, flagging prompts far from normal use
Turning off the assistant’s ability to read any documents at all
Translating every prompt into French before it is scanned
