2.why: Embeddings capture meaning rather than exact wording, so prompts far from clusters of normal usage, or close to known attacks, can be flagged even when reworded. Blocklists always lag behind.

2.q: How does threat hunting differ from alert-driven detection?
o: Hunting only happens after an incident has been confirmed
Hunters search proactively for threats that raised no alert
Hunting relies entirely on automated tools, with no analysts
Hunting replaces the need for any detection rules at all
2.why: Threat hunting is proactive and hypothesis-driven, looking for activity that detections missed, and should end in new or better detections.

2.q: Which open database and schema describe vulnerabilities in open-source packages, such as Python machine learning libraries, in machine-readable form?
o: CWE, which classifies software weakness types
OSV, an open format and database launched by Google
CAPEC, which catalogues common attack patterns
STIX, which formats shared threat intelligence
2.why: OSV provides a database and schema for open-source package vulnerabilities, mapping them to affected versions so tools can match dependencies precisely.

2.q: What is OWASP AIVSS?
o: A professional certification for AI security practitioners
An emerging vulnerability scoring system for agentic AI
A list of the ten most critical web application risks
A file format for publishing AI bills of materials
2.why: The OWASP AI Vulnerability Scoring System is an emerging approach for scoring AI risks, starting with agentic systems, where CVSS fits poorly.

2.q: Leadership wants one metric showing whether AI vulnerabilities are being fixed quickly enough, by priority. Which metric is BEST?
o: The total number of AI vulnerabilities found during the year
Mean time to remediate, measured from discovery to a verified fix
The number of vulnerability scanners the team holds licences for
The share of vulnerabilities that external researchers found
2.why: Mean time to remediate, tracked by priority and compared with targets, shows how quickly vulnerabilities are actually fixed. Counts of findings or tools say nothing about speed.

2.q: Which practice uses automated tests to confirm, continuously, that key security controls on AI systems are actually operating?
o: Annual audits, which review controls once a year
Continuous control monitoring, as part of posture assurance
Threat modelling, which identifies threats at design time
Penetration testing, which simulates attacks periodically
2.why: Continuous control monitoring checks that controls operate, not just that they are designed, giving ongoing assurance between audits.

2.q: A misconfigured AI assistant showed customers each other’s order histories for six hours. What should the privacy team do FIRST under the GDPR?
o: Wait until the full investigation is complete before deciding anything
Assess the risk at once, ready to tell the regulator within 72 hours
Email every customer, before establishing what actually happened
Treat it as a technical fault, not a breach, as no attacker was involved
2.why: Unauthorised disclosure of personal data is a personal data breach even without an attacker. The controller must assess the risk and, unless it is unlikely to harm individuals, notify the supervisory authority within 72 hours of becoming aware, and tell individuals if the risk is high.

2.q: A high-risk AI triage system in an EU hospital malfunctions, and a patient is seriously harmed as a result. Which obligation MOST directly applies to the system’s provider?
o: Publishing a press release within one week of the event
Reporting a serious incident to the market surveillance authority
Registering the system again in the EU database before further use
Waiting for the hospital to complete its own investigation first
2.why: A malfunction that seriously harms a person’s health is a serious incident. The provider must report it to the market surveillance authority, normally within 15 days of becoming aware (sooner for deaths or widespread infringements), then investigate and take corrective action.

2.q: An employee uses a company coding agent, with its broad network access, to scan internal systems outside their role. Which incident category fits BEST?
o: Model theft, copying a model’s weights or behaviour
Agent misuse, turning its permissions to harmful ends
Data poisoning, corrupting the data used for training
Hallucination, where the model invents false content
2.why: Agent misuse covers an agent’s tools and permissions being used to cause harm, whether through manipulation, error or a person abusing it.

2.q: Two AI incidents occur on the same day. One affects a single internal test assistant; the other is spreading through a shared index used by every customer-facing agent, and will persist until cleaned. Which basis for judging severity is BEST?
o: Which team happened to report its incident first
Impact, spread and persistence, which put the second far higher
The technique used, since injection always outranks other types
None: every AI incident should receive the same priority
2.why: Severity ratings combine impact, spread and persistence to drive escalation and containment. A persistent, spreading compromise of customer-facing agents outranks an isolated test system.

2.q: Why should an organisation adopt a shared AI incident taxonomy, with categories such as injection, poisoning, model theft and agent misuse?
o: So that every AI incident is handled by the same person
So incidents are triaged, routed and reported consistently
So that regulators never need to be told about incidents
So that incident response can be outsourced to vendors
2.why: A shared taxonomy makes triage, routing, metrics and reporting consistent across teams, and links categories to the right playbooks.

2.q: Which root cause analysis tool groups possible causes into categories, such as data, model, people, process, technology and suppliers?
o: A Gantt chart, which schedules tasks against time
A fishbone (Ishikawa) diagram from quality management
A RACI matrix, which assigns roles to activities
A burndown chart, which tracks remaining work
2.why: Fishbone diagrams organise possible causes by category, helping teams look beyond the model to data, process, people and suppliers.

2.q: Investigators want to estimate which training examples most affected a model’s suspicious output. Which technique fits?
o: Load testing, which measures behaviour under heavy traffic
Influence analysis, which is useful but only approximate
Penetration testing, which simulates external attacks
Model compression, which reduces the model’s size
2.why: Influence analysis estimates which training examples drove an output, helping locate poisoned data, though results are approximate.

2.q: After an AI incident, a review team wants to show each attack stage and where controls failed or held, to decide which defences to strengthen. Which approach fits BEST?
o: Listing the incident’s costs in order, from largest to smallest
Mapping it onto an AI kill chain, marking each control’s result
Writing a single-paragraph summary of the incident for the board
Counting how many log entries the incident generated per system
2.why: Mapping the incident onto a kill chain, stage by stage, shows where controls stopped or missed the attacker, guiding where to invest in prevention and detection.

2.q: Investigators suspect that only some files of a large model were altered. Which technique locates the changes?
o: Asking the model whether any of its files have been modified
Hashing each file and comparing it with the approved version
Retraining the model and checking whether its accuracy changes
Reviewing the model card for notes about recent changes
2.why: Weight comparison hashes and compares each file against the approved registry version, detecting and locating tampering.

2.q: A kill switch stops a payments agent mid-task. Afterwards, nobody can tell which payments went through, which were half-finished and which never started. Which design element was MOST clearly missing?
o: A louder alarm that sounds whenever the kill switch is pressed
A defined safe state for in-flight work, and how to resume it
A second kill switch, held by a different team for redundancy
A rule that agents may only run outside normal business hours
2.why: A kill switch must lead to a defined safe state: in-flight transactions are completed, rolled back or held, with a record of each, so recovery is orderly. Stopping without one creates new risk.

2.q: Which international standard sets out requirements for business continuity management systems?
o: ISO/IEC 27001
ISO/IEC 42001
ISO 9001
2.why: ISO 22301 specifies business continuity management systems. ISO/IEC 27001 covers information security, 42001 AI management and 9001 quality.

2.q: During a provider outage, a support service switches to a smaller in-house model with fewer features until the provider recovers. What is this?
o: A full outage, with no service available to customers
Degraded mode, a reduced but safe level of service
A rollback, restoring a previous approved model version
A cold start, rebuilding the service from scratch
2.why: Degraded mode runs a reduced but safe service, such as a smaller model or rules, while full capability is unavailable.

2.q: Which metric measures the time from detecting an AI incident to stopping further harm?
o: Mean time between failures, a reliability measure
Time to contain, a key responder performance metric
Recovery point objective, the tolerable data loss
Mean time to acknowledge, how fast alerts are seen
2.why: Time to contain measures how quickly further harm is stopped after detection. It reflects detection quality, decision rights and pre-approved actions.

2.q: Each new AI project’s threat model starts from a blank page, and different teams miss different well-known threats. What would BEST improve consistency?
o: Asking each team to spend twice as long on its threat model
A shared catalogue of common AI attacks and their mitigations
Skipping threat modelling for projects that use hosted models
Hiring an external firm to model each project once, at launch
2.why: A maintained threat library gives modellers a reusable catalogue of known threats, drawing on sources such as MITRE ATLAS and the OWASP lists, with mitigations, so common threats aren’t missed and analyses are consistent.

2.q: An attacker with only API access repeatedly queries a model and studies its outputs to craft inputs that evade it. What type of attack is this?
o: A white-box attack, using the model’s weights and gradients
A black-box attack, relying solely on the model’s responses
A supply chain attack, tampering with the model before release
An insider attack, by someone with privileged internal access
2.why: Black-box attacks use only queries and outputs. Rate limits, output minimisation and monitoring raise their cost.

2.q: Instructions hidden in an email redirect an agent from summarising messages to forwarding them to an outsider. Which agentic threat is this?
o: Rogue agent, acting outside its purpose on its own initiative
Agent goal hijack, the first risk in OWASP’s agentic list
Cascading failure, where one agent’s error spreads to others
Capacity exhaustion, where demand overwhelms the agent
2.why: Agent goal hijack (ASI01) manipulates an agent’s objectives through injected content. Limit what untrusted content can trigger, and require approval for sensitive actions.

2.q: An agent starts acting outside its intended purpose and control, for example creating accounts and scheduling tasks nobody asked for. What is this called?
o: Agent goal hijack, where injected content redirects its aims
A rogue agent, which needs containment and investigation
Excessive autonomy, where it acts without human review
Model drift, where its accuracy declines over time
2.why: A rogue agent acts outside its intended purpose or control (OWASP ASI10). Kill switches, monitoring and least privilege limit the damage.

2.q: One tenant’s heavy AI workloads keep exhausting a shared inference service, slowing every other tenant. Which control addresses this MOST directly?
o: A longer system prompt asking tenants to use less capacity
Capacity isolation, with per-tenant quotas and reserved capacity
Moving every tenant to the same larger shared GPU pool
Removing monitoring, so that the service runs more efficiently
2.why: Capacity isolation, through per-tenant quotas, priorities and reserved capacity, stops one tenant’s load from denying service to others.

2.q: Small stickers on a stop sign make a vision model read it as a speed limit sign, though people still see a normal stop sign. What does the altered sign represent?
o: A backdoor trigger, planted during the model’s training
An adversarial example, crafted to mislead the model
A hallucination, where the model invents an object
A data drift event, caused by changes in the input mix
2.why: Adversarial examples are inputs with small, deliberate changes that cause misclassification at inference, without any access to training.

2.q: Which international standard defines AI system lifecycle processes, building on established software lifecycle standards?
o: ISO/IEC 27001
ISO/IEC 5338
ISO/IEC 29147
2.why: ISO/IEC 5338 defines AI system lifecycle processes, extending ISO/IEC/IEEE 12207 and 15288 for AI-specific needs.

2.q: What MOST distinguishes an A/B test from a canary release?
o: A/B tests are always run in production; canaries never are
A/B tests compare variants’ outcomes; canaries limit risk exposure
They are the same practice, described by different teams
A/B tests need no monitoring; canaries need constant monitoring
2.why: A/B tests split traffic to compare variants on business or quality outcomes. Canary releases expose a small group first, to catch problems safely.

2.q: A team wants to add a new external website as a retrieval source for its customer assistant. The change isn’t pre-approved and isn’t urgent. Which approach is BEST?
o: Treat it as a standard change, deployed at once without review
Treat it as a normal change, assessed and approved before release
Treat it as an emergency change, approved after it goes live
Keep it outside change management, since sources aren’t code
2.why: A new retrieval source changes what the model reads, including possible injection paths, so it needs a normal change: risk assessment and approval before release. Standard changes are pre-approved and low risk; emergency changes are for urgent fixes.

2.q: What does the UK government’s AI Cyber Security Code of Practice set out?
o: Mandatory fines for AI companies that suffer data breaches
Voluntary baseline principles across the whole AI lifecycle
A licensing scheme that all AI models must pass before sale
Technical rules for the UK’s critical national infrastructure
2.why: The voluntary code sets baseline security principles for developers and operators across the AI lifecycle, and formed the basis of ETSI TS 104 223.

2.q: What does ISO/IEC 42006 cover?
o: Requirements for AI management systems within organisations
Requirements for bodies that certify AI management systems
Guidance on managing the risks that AI systems create
Requirements for carrying out AI system impact assessments
2.why: ISO/IEC 42006 sets requirements for audit and certification bodies, raising confidence in ISO/IEC 42001 certificates. 42001 is the management system, 23894 covers risk and 42005 impact assessment.

2.q: After verifying a third-party model on intake, a company signs it with its own key, so internal deployment gates need to trust only one signer. What is this practice?
o: Keyless signing, using short-lived certificates from a public CA
Counter-signing, recording that the intake checks passed
Code obfuscation, hiding how the model’s files are structured
Watermarking, embedding a mark in the model’s behaviour
2.why: Counter-signing records that the organisation verified an artefact on entry, so internal gates can rely on one trusted internal signature.

2.q: An AI vendor offers only a one-page letter confirming that a penetration test took place, not the report. The service will process sensitive customer data. What is the BEST next step for the assessor?
o: Accept the letter, since it confirms independent testing happened
Request the scope, key findings and remediation status, under NDA
Reject the vendor outright, without asking for anything further
Run an unauthorised penetration test of the vendor’s service
2.why: An attestation letter confirms testing happened, but not its scope, findings or fixes. For sensitive data, ask for the report or a summary of scope, findings and remediation, under NDA if needed. Never test a vendor without authorisation.

2.q: A SOC 2 report uses the inclusive method for the AI vendor’s model hosting subservice provider. What does this mean?
o: The provider’s controls are excluded, so separate evidence is needed
The provider’s relevant controls are within the report’s scope
The provider is a competitor, so it isn’t mentioned at all
The provider’s staff wrote the report on the vendor’s behalf
2.why: Under the inclusive method, a subservice organisation’s relevant controls are included and tested. Under the carve-out method, they are excluded and need separate assurance.

2.q: Which open-source tool, now maintained by NVIDIA, probes LLMs for weaknesses such as jailbreaks, prompt injection and data leakage, using many built-in probes?
o: Wireshark, which captures and analyses network traffic
garak, a scanner built specifically for language models
Nmap, which discovers hosts and open network ports
Burp Suite, which tests web applications for flaws
2.why: garak probes LLMs with many attack types. PyRIT and promptfoo are other common tools; Wireshark, Nmap and Burp target networks and web apps.

2.q: A red team plan lists scenarios such as “try to break the chatbot”, with no further detail, and results can’t be compared between rounds. What is the BEST improvement?
o: Letting testers choose freely, so their creativity isn’t constrained
Defining each scenario’s objective, target, technique and success test
Reducing the plan to a single scenario in each round of testing
Running the same broad scenarios again with more testers
2.why: Well-defined scenarios state the objective, target, technique class and evidence of success, so results are repeatable, comparable between rounds and traceable to risks.

2.q: In DARPA’s AI Cyber Challenge (AIxCC), what were the competing cyber reasoning systems designed to do?
o: Write marketing copy for cyber security products
Find and fix software vulnerabilities autonomously
Detect deepfake videos in social media feeds
Train new security analysts using simulations
2.why: Cyber reasoning systems autonomously find and patch vulnerabilities. The AIxCC finalists’ systems found and fixed real flaws in open-source software.

2.q: Which publication offers a structured approach to red teaming generative AI, covering model evaluation, implementation, infrastructure and runtime behaviour?
o: The OWASP Top 10 for web applications
The OWASP GenAI Red Teaming Guide
The CIS Benchmarks for Kubernetes

2.why: The OWASP GenAI Red Teaming Guide covers model evaluation, implementation testing, infrastructure and runtime behaviour, with practical methods.

2.q: A company’s annual penetration test of its AI assistant found no infrastructure flaws, so leadership believes the assistant is secure. What is the BEST response?
o: Agree, since penetration tests cover every aspect of AI risk
Add AI red teaming to test model behaviour, misuse and harms
Repeat the same penetration test monthly instead of annually
Replace the assistant with a rules-based chatbot to remove the risk
2.why: Traditional penetration tests focus on infrastructure and application flaws. AI red teaming also probes model behaviour, such as jailbreaks, injection, harmful outputs and misuse, which a clean penetration test doesn’t rule out.

2.q: Developers keep rejecting AI red team findings as unclear, and some findings are lost between teams. Which change BEST fixes this?
o: A one-line title for each finding, so they are quicker to read
Records with description, component, evidence, severity, owner, status
Adding the tester’s view of each developer’s skill to the record
A screenshot of the final response only, without any other context
2.why: A complete finding record gives developers what they need to reproduce and fix the issue, and gives managers ownership and status tracking, so findings aren’t lost or disputed.

2.q: A high-severity AI finding can’t be fixed before a fixed launch date, and the product owner wants to launch anyway. What is the BEST course of action?
o: Launch quietly, and leave the finding out of the final report
A time-limited risk acceptance by the accountable owner, with controls
Downgrade the finding to low severity, so that the launch can proceed
Delay every other project until this one finding has been fixed
2.why: If a finding can’t be fixed in time, the accountable owner can formally accept the risk for a limited period, with compensating controls and a remediation date. Hiding or downgrading findings undermines the assessment.

2.q: A data-leak finding reproduces in only 3 of 100 attempts. How should it be treated?
o: Closed, as it can’t be reproduced reliably
As real: rare successes still matter at scale
Ignored, unless attackers are seen using it
As a model limitation, not a security issue
2.why: AI findings are probabilistic. A 3% success rate across thousands of interactions means many successes, so record the rate and treat the finding as real.

2.q: A tester rates every jailbreak finding as critical, whatever it achieves, and developers have started ignoring the ratings. What is the BEST correction?
o: Rate every finding as medium, to avoid alarming the developers
Base severity on impact and exploitability, not the technique used
Stop rating findings, and send developers raw transcripts instead
Let developers set each finding’s severity in their own systems
2.why: Severity should reflect what a finding achieves and how easily, using a consistent rubric. Inflating everything to critical destroys the signal and slows the fixes that matter.

2.q: A privileged model writes a short program in a restricted language, so the flow of untrusted data can be tracked and checked before anything runs. Which pattern is this?
o: The action-selector pattern, which never reads tool outputs
The code-then-execute pattern, among the six design patterns
The LLM map-reduce pattern, isolating each untrusted item
The plan-then-execute pattern, fixing actions in advance
2.why: In code-then-execute, the plan becomes a program in a restricted language, letting the system track untrusted data and enforce policies on its use.

2.q: An assistant summarises 500 untrusted customer reviews by processing each one in an isolated worker and combining only constrained results. Which pattern is this?
o: The action-selector pattern, choosing from fixed actions
The LLM map-reduce pattern, limiting each item’s influence
The dual LLM pattern, with privileged and quarantined models
The context minimisation pattern, removing unneeded content
2.why: The LLM map-reduce pattern processes each untrusted item in isolation and combines only constrained outputs, so one malicious item can’t steer the rest.

2.q: A team wants to defend a model against universal jailbreaks on one high-risk topic, while keeping false refusals low. Which approach has published research shown to be MOST effective?
o: A longer system prompt listing every request that is forbidden
Input and output classifiers trained from a written set of principles
Lowering the model’s temperature, so its outputs become deterministic
Blocking every prompt that is longer than 200 characters in total
2.why: Anthropic’s Constitutional Classifiers, trained on synthetic data generated from a constitution, cut automated jailbreak success from 86% to 4.4% with only a small rise in refusals. System prompts and temperature changes don’t stop determined attacks.

2.q: A content classifier is being evaded by inputs with small, carefully crafted perturbations, and the team can’t retrain the model this quarter. Which mitigation is BEST to apply in the meantime?
o: Publishing the model’s weights so that researchers can study it
Input preprocessing, such as re-encoding or paraphrasing them
Increasing the precision of the scores the API returns to clients
Removing all logging, to improve the service’s response times
2.why: Transforming inputs before inference, such as re-encoding, compression or paraphrasing, can break up adversarial patterns without retraining. It isn’t a complete defence, since adaptive attacks can account for it, so pair it with monitoring and plan adversarial training.
